swapToAskAbout.text: Methylphenidate also comes in immediate-release and liquid forms. Guidelines say asking the pharmacist about one of these is often worthwhile.

draft.verdict: Metadate CD is an extended-release capsule, and short bowel guidelines generally avoid this kind of medicine after a large bowel removal, so it may not fully work in your body.

why.claim: Metadate CD is an extended-release capsule.
The label says not to crush or chew the capsule or what is inside it.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, slow-release and delayed-release medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal gut to release the drug.
When the bowel is short or food moves through fast, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the colon. Without a colon, they have less time and less surface to do that.
How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. You have under 100 cm.

draft.verdict: Dulcolax tablets are a delayed-release (coated) tablet, and guidelines say this kind of tablet is generally avoided after a large small-bowel resection like yours, so please check with your care team before using them.

why.claim: The Dulcolax-type bisacodyl tablet label lists the form as a delayed-release tablet.
After a large small-bowel resection, delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines are generally avoided because they need a long, normal gut to release the drug.
When things move through fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets pass through whole.
Enteric-coated products are in the highest-risk group for not dissolving in people with an ostomy.
Laxatives can add to the risk of dehydration and low sodium in people with a stoma.

The first record I was given for 'Dulcolax' was a different product (a powder with polyethylene glycol 3350), so I looked up the bisacodyl tablet label separately. That label had no detailed sections, so I could not read its directions.

draft.verdict: Venlafaxine ER is an extended-release tablet, and the guidelines say this kind of tablet is generally avoided with a short bowel and no colon, because some of the dose may pass out before it is released.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow each tablet whole with fluid, and not to divide, crush, chew, or put it in water.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, sustained-release medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal gut transit to release the drug.
With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the colon. Without a colon, they have less time and surface to do it.
In ostomy patients, extended-release products are grouped as a 'critical' dissolution risk.
The tablet lists mannitol as an inactive ingredient. Mannitol is a sugar alcohol.
Sugar alcohols like mannitol are poorly absorbed. They pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.

draft.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked saying chlorhexidine 0.12% oral rinse won't work with an end-jejunostomy, but the label I found didn't include its directions, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: I found the label under the name "chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12% oral rinse". It is a liquid, not a tablet, so there is no coating or slow-release form to worry about.
The label says the gut takes in very little chlorhexidine gluconate.
Liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol, which pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
The ingredient list shows chlorhexidine gluconate, water, alcohol, glycerin and PEG-40 sorbitan diisostearate. Sorbitol is not on the list.
The label I found had no directions section or patient leaflet. That means I couldn't check what it says about swallowing the rinse. Ask your pharmacist.

why.claim: This product is a tablet. The checked label lists it as immediate-release, not extended-release or coated.
Most medicines are absorbed in the first part of the small bowel, the jejunum. Many plain immediate-release medicines can still be absorbed when that part is still there.
Plain tablets that dissolve fast are grouped as low-risk for not dissolving in people with an ostomy. Extended-release and coated tablets are the higher-risk group.
How well a medicine absorbs depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. With under 100 cm, that's a real question.
In studies, 29 of 37 medicines were absorbed less after bowel surgery, and 6 stopped working well enough. It differs from drug to drug, so no one can give you a single number.

For medicines where the gap between too little and too much is small, doctors may check blood levels or watch closely how well the medicine is working, because absorption after bowel surgery is hard to predict.
The label says food and antacids do not change how this medicine is absorbed.
The inactive ingredients listed include croscarmellose sodium and hydrogenated vegetable oil. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohols are listed.

draft.verdict: This is a plain immediate-release tablet, and I found nothing in the sources I checked that says to avoid it with your anatomy, but with under 100 cm of bowel it's worth confirming with your pharmacist that it's absorbed well.

why.claim: The label I found lists it as a tablet, and the drug table says it is immediate-release, not extended-release or coated.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, the first part of the jejunum. Plain immediate-release medicines can often still be absorbed if that part is still there.
Plain tablets that dissolve fast are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving in people with an ostomy. Extended-release and coated products carry the most risk.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is. With under 100 cm, how much gets absorbed can vary from person to person.
The label says acetaminophen is quickly absorbed from the gut.
The label says the tablets contain inactive ingredients, but the list itself was missing from the label I found. So I couldn't fully check for sugar alcohols like sorbitol, which can raise output.
There is also a liquid version on the market. Liquids may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

why.claim: Effexor XR is an extended-release capsule.

draft.ask: ASK: I have an ileostomy and my colon isn't connected. Will this extended-release tramadol release fully in my gut, or would a different form work better for me?

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask whether a plain, fast-dissolving (immediate-release) form of this pain medicine could suit your body better. Only your prescriber can decide this.

draft.verdict: This is an extended-release tablet, and without a connected colon some of the dose may leave through your ileostomy before it is fully released, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.

The label says to swallow it whole. It warns that crushing, chewing, splitting or dissolving it releases the drug in an uncontrolled way and can lead to overdose or death. Please don't change how you take it on your own.
Slow-release tablets need enough time moving through the gut to release their medicine. If the gut is shorter or moves faster, some of the dose may leave the body first.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the large bowel. Your colon is not connected, so the tablet has less time and less gut lining to release in.
Extended-release products are grouped as 'critical', meaning higher risk of not dissolving properly in people with an ostomy.
How well medicines are absorbed depends more on how much healthy small bowel is left than on the type of stoma. You have over 200 cm, which your team can factor in.
The label also says tramadol slows the gut and reduces pushing movements in the small intestine.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING ADDICTION, ABUSE, AND MISUSE; RISK EVALUATION AND MITIGATION STRATEGY (REMS); LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION; ACCIDENTAL INGESTION; ULTRA-RAPID METABOLISM OF TRAMADOL AND OTHER RISK FACTORS FOR LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION IN CHILDREN; NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME; INTERACTIONS WITH DRUGS AFFECTING CYTOCHROME P450 ISOENZYMES; AND RISKS FROM CONCOMITANT USE WITH BENZODIAZEPINES OR OTHER CNS DEPRESSENTS Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse Because the use of Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablet exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death, assess each patient's risk prior to prescribing and reassess all patients regularly for the development of these behaviors and conditions [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1)]. Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, especially during initiation or following a dose increase. To reduce the risk of respiratory depression, proper dosing and titration of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets are essential. [see Warnings and Precautions (5.2)]. Accidental Ingestion Accidental ingestion of even one dose of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, especially by children, can result in a fatal overdose of tramadol [see Warnings and Precautions (5.2)]. Risks From Concomitant Use With Benzodiazepines Or Other CNS Depressants Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets and benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3), Drug Interactions (7)]. Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome If opioid use is required for an extended period of time in a pregnant woman, advise the patient of the risk of NOWS, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Ensure that management by neonatology experts will be available at delivery[see Warnings and Precautions (5.4)]. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12.1 Mechanism of Action Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablet contains tramadol, an opioid agonist and an inhibitor of reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Although the mode of action of tramadol is not completely understood, the analgesic effect of tramadol is believed to be due to both binding to µ-opioid receptors and weak inhibition of reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Opioid activity of tramadol is due to both low affinity binding of the parent compound and higher affinity binding of the O-desmethyl metabolite M1 to µ-opioid receptors. In animal models, M1 is up to 6 times more potent than tramadol in producing analgesia and 200 times more potent in µ-opioid binding. Tramadol-induced analgesia is only partially antagonized by the opioid antagonist naloxone in several animal tests. The relative contribution of both tramadol and M1 to human analgesia is dependent upon the plasma concentrations of each compound. Tramadol has been shown to inhibit reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin in vitro, as have some other opioid analgesics. These mechanisms may contribute independently to the overall analgesic profile of tramadol. Apart from analgesia, tramadol administration may produce a constellation of symptoms (including dizziness, somnolence, nausea, constipation, sweating and pruritus) similar to that of other opioids. In contrast to morphine, tramadol has not been shown to cause histamine release. At therapeutic doses, tramadol has no effect on heart rate, left-ventricular function, or cardiac index. Orthostatic hypotension has been observed. 12.2 Pharmacodynamics Effects on the Central Nervous System Tramadol produces respiratory depression by direct action on brain stem respiratory centers. The respiratory depression involves a reduction in the responsiveness of the brain stem respiratory centers to both increases in carbon dioxide tension and electrical stimulation. Tramadol causes miosis, even in total darkness. Pinpoint pupils are a sign of opioid overdose but are not pathognomonic (e.g., pontine lesions of hemorrhagic or ischemic origins may produce similar findings). Marked mydriasis rather than miosis may be seen due to hypoxia in overdose situations. Effects on the Gastrointestinal Tract and Other Smooth Muscle Tramadol causes a reduction in motility associated with an increase in smooth muscle tone in the antrum of the stomach and duodenum. Digestion of food in the small intestine is delayed and propulsive contractions are decreased. Propulsive peristaltic waves in the colon are decreased, while tone may be increased to the point of spasm, resulting in constipation. Other opioid-induced effects may include a reduction in biliary and pancreatic secretions, spasm of sphincter of Oddi, and transient elevations in serum amylase. Effects on the Cardiovascular System Tramadol produces peripheral vasodilation, which may result in orthostatic hypotension or syncope. Manifestations of histamine release and/or peripheral vasodilation may include pruritus, flushing, red eyes, sweating, and/or orthostatic hypotension. The effect of oral tramadol on the QTcF interval was evaluated in a double-blind, randomized, four-way crossover, placebo- and positive- (moxifloxacin) controlled study in 68 adult male and female healthy subjects. At a 600 mg/day dose (1.5-fold the maximum immediate-release daily dose), the study demonstrated no significant effect on the QTcF interval. Effects on the Endocrine System Opioids inhibit the secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), cortisol, and luteinizing hormone (LH) in humans [see Adverse Reactions (6.2)]. They also stimulate prolactin, growth hormone (GH) secretion, and pancreatic secretion of insulin and glucagon. Use of opioids for an extended period of time may influence the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, leading to androgen deficiency that may manifest as low libido, impotence, erectile dysfunction, amenorrhea, or infertility. evidence.L:description: Tramadol hydrochloride is an opioid agonist in an extended-release tablet formulation for oral use. The chemical name is (±) cis-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-(3-methoxyphenyl) cyclohexanol hydrochloride. Its structural formula is: [image-1] The molecular weight of tramadol HCl is 299.84. It is a white, bitter, crystalline and odorless powder that is readily soluble in water and ethanol and has a pKa of 9.41. The n-octanol/water log partition coefficient (logP) is 1.35 at pH 7. Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets USP contain 100, 200 or 300 mg of tramadol HCl in an extended-release formulation. The tablets are white to off-white in color and contain the inactive ingredients: colloidal silicon dioxide, dibutyl sebacate, ethyl cellulose, microcrystalline cellulose, povidone, and sodium stearyl fumarate. The imprinting ink contains shellac, iron oxide black and propylene glycol. Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets USP meet USP Dissolution Test 3.
evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2.1 Important Dosage and Administration Instructions Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable about the use of extended-release/long-acting opioids and how to mitigate the associated risks. Do not use tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets concomitantly with other tramadol products [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3), (5.15)]. Do not administer tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets at a dose exceeding 300 mg per day. Use the lowest effective dosage for the shortest duration of time consistent with individual patient treatment goals [see Warnings and Precautions (5.5)]. Because the risk of overdose increases as opioid doses increase, reserve titration to higher doses of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets for patients in whom lower doses are insufficiently effective and in whom the expected benefits of using a higher dose opioid clearly outweigh the substantial risks. Initiate the dosing regimen for each patient individually, taking into account the patient's underlying cause and severity of pain, prior analgesic treatment and response, and risk factors for addiction, abuse, and misuse [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1)] Respiratory depression can occur at any time during opioid therapy, especially when initiating and following dosage increases with tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets. Consider this risk when selecting an initial dose and when making dose adjustments [see Warnings and Precautions (5.5)]. Instruct patients to swallow tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets whole [see Patient Counseling Information (17)], and to take it with liquid. Crushing, chewing, splitting, or dissolving tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets will result in uncontrolled delivery of tramadol and can lead to overdose or death [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1)]. Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets may be taken without regard to food, It is recommended that tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets be taken in a consistent manner [see Clinical Pharmacology (12.3)]. 2.2 Patient Access to Naloxone for the Emergency Treatment of Opioid Overdose Discuss the availability of naloxone for the emergency treatment of opioid overdose with the patient and caregiver and assess the potential need for access to naloxone, both when initiating and renewing treatment with tramadol hydrochloride extended release tablets [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3), Patient Counseling Information (17)]. Inform patients and caregivers about the various ways to obtain naloxone as permitted by individual state naloxone dispensing and prescribing requirements or guidelines (e.g., by prescription, directly from a pharmacist, or as part of a community-based program). Consider prescribing naloxone, based on the patient's risk factors for overdose, such as concomitant use of CNS depressants, a history of opioid use disorder, or prior opioid overdose. The presence of risk factors for overdose should not prevent the proper management of pain in any given patient [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1, 5.3, 5.7)]. Consider prescribing naloxone if the patient has household members (including children) or other close contacts at risk for accidental ingestion or overdose. 2.3 Initial Dosage Patients Not Currently on a Tramadol Product The initial dose of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets is 100 mg once daily. Storage and Disposal: Because of the risks associated with accidental ingestion, misuse, and abuse, advise patients to store tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets securely, out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1), Drug Abuse and Dependence (9)]. Inform patients that leaving tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets unsecured can pose a deadly risk to others in the home. Advise patients and caregivers that when medicines are no longer needed, they should be disposed of promptly. Inform patients that medicine take-back options are the preferred way to safely dispose of most types of unneeded medicines. If no take back programs or DEA-registered collectors are available, instruct patients to dispose of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets by following these four steps: Mix tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets (do not crush) with an unpalatable substance such as dirt, cat litter, or used coffee grounds; Place the mixture in a container such as a sealed plastic bag; Throw the container in the household trash; Delete all personal information on the prescription label of the empty bottle Inform patients that they can visit www.fda.gov/drugdisposal for additional information on disposal of unused medicines. Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse Inform patients that the use of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, even when taken as recommended, can result in addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1)]. Instruct patients not to share tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets with others and to take steps to protect tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets from theft or misuse. Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression Inform patients of the risk of life-threatening respiratory depression, including information that the risk is greatest when starting tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets or when the dosage is increased, and that it can occur even at recommended dosages . Advise patients how to recognize respiratory depression and to seek medical attention if breathing difficulties develop. Educate patients and caregivers on how to recognize respiratory depression and emphasize the importance of calling 911 or getting emergency medical help right away in the event of a known or suspected overdose [see Warnings and Precautions (5.2)]. Accidental Ingestion Inform patients that accidental ingestion, especially by children, may result in respiratory depression or death [see Warnings and Precautions (5.2)]. Interactions with Benzodiazepines and Other CNS Depressants Inform patients and caregivers that potentially fatal additive effects may occur if tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets are used with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, and not to use these concomitantly unless supervised by a healthcare provider [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3), Drug Interactions (7)]. evidence.L:warnings_and_cautions: 5.1 Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse Tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablet contains tramadol, a Schedule IV controlled substance. As an opioid, tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablet exposes users to the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse. Because extended-release products such as tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets deliver the opioid over an extended period of time, there is a greater risk for overdose and death due to the larger amount of tramadol present [see Drug Abuse and Dependence(9)]. Although the risk of addiction in any individual is unknown, it can occur in patients appropriately prescribed tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets. Addiction can occur at recommended dosages and if the drug is misused or abused. Assess each patient's risk for opioid addiction, abuse, or misuse prior to prescribing tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, and reassess all patients receiving tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets for the development of these behaviors and conditions. Risks are increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depression). The potential for these risks should not, however, prevent the proper management of pain in any given patient. Patients at increased risk may be prescribed opioids such as tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, but use in such patients necessitates intensive counseling about the risks and proper use of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets along with frequent reevaluation for signs of addiction, abuse, and misuse. Consider prescribing naloxone for the emergency treatment of opioid overdose [see Dosage and Administration (2.2), Warnings and Precautions (5.3)]. Abuse or misuse of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets by cutting, breaking, chewing, crushing, snorting, or injecting the dissolved product will result in the uncontrolled delivery of tramadol and can result in overdose and death [see Overdosage (10)]. Opioids are sought for non-medical use and are subject to diversion from legitimate prescribed use. Consider these risks when prescribing or dispensing tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets. Strategies to reduce these risks include prescribing the drug in the smallest appropriate quantity and advising the patient on careful storage of the drug during the course of treatment and proper disposal of unused drug. Contact local state professional licensing board or state-controlled substances authority for information on how to prevent and detect abuse or diversion of this product. 5.2 Life Threatening Respiratory Depression Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression has been reported with the use of opioids, even when used as recommended. Respiratory depression, if not immediately recognized and treated, may lead to respiratory arrest and death. Management of respiratory depression may include close observation, supportive measures, and use of opioid antagonists, depending on the patient's clinical status [see Overdosage (10)]. Carbon dioxide (CO2) retention from opioid-induced respiratory depression can exacerbate the sedating effects of opioids. While serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression can occur at any time during the use of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets, the risk is greatest during the initiation of therapy or following a dosage increase of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets. To reduce the risk of respiratory depression, proper dosing and titration of tramadol hydrochloride extended-release tablets are essential [see Dosage and Administration (2)]. swapToAskAbout.text: You could ask whether a form that does not rely on slow release would suit your body better. In the ostomy study, solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets were the lowest-risk group. This is a question for your care team to decide, not a change to make yourself.

draft.verdict: Xtampza ER is an extended-release capsule, and without a colon in use, part of the dose may not have enough time to be released, so this is worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: Xtampza ER is an extended-release capsule.
Slow-release products like this need time in the gut. When the gut is shorter or moves fast, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the colon. Your colon is not connected, so there is less time and surface for release.
A study of ostomy patients put extended-release products in the highest-risk group for not dissolving properly.
How well medicines are absorbed depends more on how much healthy small bowel is left than on the type of stoma. Your over 200 cm of small bowel may help, but it does not remove the concern.
The label says your body takes up more of the medicine when it is taken with food than on an empty stomach.

draft.ask: ASK: I have an end-jejunostomy with under 100 cm of bowel. Does this fluoxetine solution contain sorbitol or other sugar alcohols, and how will we know it's being absorbed?
sourcesChecked: Guidelines: liquid medicines, sugar alcohols, drug absorption after resection
draft.verdict: A liquid is often the easier form for a short bowel, but how much fluoxetine you absorb with under 100 cm of bowel is hard to predict, and I couldn't see the full ingredient list.

why.claim: This product is a liquid, not a time-release or coated pill.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome.
But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol. These pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
The label text I got lists alcohol 0.23% and benzoic acid, then cuts off. The separate inactive ingredients section was missing, so I can't confirm there are no sugar alcohols.
Food may delay absorption by 1 to 2 hours but does not appear to change how much is absorbed. The label doesn't say where in the gut fluoxetine is absorbed.
After bowel surgery, absorption dropped for most drugs studied. The effect differs from drug to drug, so it can't be predicted for one person.
How well pills and liquids are absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left, more than on the type of stoma.
The guidelines say that when a medicine doesn't seem to work as expected, poor absorption should be suspected and is worth bringing up with the prescriber or pharmacist.

final.verdict: A liquid may be absorbed more reliably than tablets with a short bowel, but how much fluoxetine you absorb with under 100 cm of bowel is hard to predict, and I couldn't see the full ingredient list.

why.claim: This product is a liquid.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome.
But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol. These pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
The label text I got lists alcohol 0.23% and benzoic acid, then cuts off. The separate inactive ingredients section was missing, so I can't confirm there are no sugar alcohols.
Food may delay absorption by 1 to 2 hours but does not appear to change how much is absorbed. The label doesn't say where in the gut fluoxetine is absorbed.
After bowel surgery, absorption dropped for most drugs studied. The effect differs from drug to drug, so it can't be predicted for one person.
How well oral medicines are absorbed depends mostly on the length and health of the remaining small bowel, more than on the type of stoma.
The guidelines say that when a medicine doesn't seem to work as expected, poor absorption should be suspected and raised with the prescriber or pharmacist.

why.claim: Jylamvo is a liquid solution. It is not a tablet that has to dissolve first.
Guidelines group solutions as 'noncritical' for dissolution problems in people with an ostomy.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
After a lot of small bowel is removed, extended-release and delayed-release medicines are usually avoided. They need a long, normal gut to let the drug out.
With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release tablets may let out part of their dose in the colon. Your colon is not connected, so the tablet has less time and less gut to work in.
The label says to swallow it whole and not break, crush, dissolve, chew or cut it. So changing how you take it is not a fix to try on your own.

The ingredients listed on the label are polyethylene glycol, hypromellose and magnesium stearate. The label does not list sorbitol. The separate inactive ingredient and warnings sections were missing from the label I could check.

If you ever see a whole tablet or shell in your pouch, it could mean the medicine did not dissolve. It could also be an empty shell left after the drug came out. Either way, show it to your pharmacist.

draft.verdict: Khindivi is a liquid, and liquids are usually the easier form for an ileostomy to absorb. The one open question is that I could only see part of its inactive ingredient list, so I can't confirm it has no sugar alcohols, which can raise stoma output.

why.claim: Khindivi is a solution (a liquid), not a tablet or capsule.

In people with an ostomy, solutions are in the 'noncritical' group, meaning the medicine does not need to break down in the gut first. Extended-release and enteric-coated products are the risky group.
Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome. But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
Sugar alcohols like sorbitol, xylitol and mannitol pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.

The label lists some inactive ingredients (berry flavor, butylated hydroxyanisole, ethyl maltol), but the text I got was cut off. The full inactive-ingredient section was missing, so I couldn't check the whole list.
The label says a high-fat meal made no meaningful difference to how the body takes up Khindivi.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium. Anything that raises output is worth watching.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole, without crushing, chewing or sucking.
The label says the potassium is fully absorbed before it leaves the small intestine. That statement is about a full-length gut, and you have under 100 cm of small bowel.
Time-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel to release their drug. When the bowel is shorter or moves things through faster, part of the dose may leave before it is released.
Guidelines generally avoid sustained-release and delayed-release medicines after extensive small-bowel resection.
An immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often worth asking the pharmacist about. Potassium chloride also comes in immediate-release and liquid forms.
Liquid medicines can be absorbed more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can make diarrhea or output worse. If you switch, ask about the ingredients.
Of 13 people with your anatomy who logged this tablet, 2 said it helped, 9 noticed no change and 2 said it caused problems.

draft.ask: ASK: I have an ileostomy and dehydrate easily. How should my fluids, sodium and potassium be checked while I take this spironolactone suspension?
sourcesChecked: Guidelines: liquid medicines, sugar alcohols, release forms
Guidelines: diuretics and dehydration with an ileostomy
draft.verdict: The liquid form should be a good fit for absorption after resection, but spironolactone is a diuretic (water pill), and guidelines say diuretics can raise the risk of dehydration and low sodium for people with an ileostomy.

why.claim: This product is a liquid suspension, not an extended-release or coated tablet.
Liquids are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving problems in people with an ostomy. Extended-release and enteric-coated products are the high-risk group.
Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium. Diuretics like spironolactone can add to that risk.
Tell your care team quickly if you notice warning signs: thirst, dark or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, or more stoma output.
Liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol, which can raise stoma output.

The part of the label I could see lists sorbic acid, potassium sorbate and citric acid. None of these are sugar alcohols. But the full list of inactive ingredients was missing, so I could not check every ingredient.
A high-fat meal raised how much spironolactone the body took in by about 90%. So taking it with or without food can change how much you get.

draft.verdict: Asacol HD is a delayed-release coated tablet, and guidelines say this kind of tablet may not release its medicine properly in a short bowel, so please check it with your care team.

why.claim: This medicine (mesalamine) comes as a delayed-release tablet.

The tablet has a coating that breaks down only at pH 6.8 or higher. That normally happens in the last part of the small bowel (the terminal ileum). Only then does the medicine start to come out of the tablet.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines are usually avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
When food and pills move through fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets pass through whole.
The label says to swallow the tablet whole and not split or crush it. So please don't change how you take it on your own. Ask first.
How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. You have less than 100 cm.
One caution: the label I found under this name is for Lialda, a different brand of delayed-release mesalamine. It is not the Asacol HD label itself, and its full inactive ingredient list was missing.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask whether there is a form of sucralfate without sorbitol that would work for you. Sugar alcohols in liquid medicines can raise output.

draft.verdict: Your body can likely handle Carafate suspension's liquid form, but it contains sorbitol, which can loosen output, so it's worth a quick check with your pharmacist.

why.claim: The label lists sorbitol solution as an ingredient in Carafate Oral Suspension.
Sorbitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed. They pull water into the gut and can increase stoma output or diarrhea. They often show up in liquid medicines.
Liquids are in the lowest-risk group for not dissolving in people with an ostomy, so the form itself is not the worry.
The label says very little sucralfate is absorbed from the gut.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, and medicines are often absorbed normally. Stoma type alone is not a guarantee, though.
With your colon still connected, your colon absorbs water and salt. That may soften the effect of extra water in the gut.

final.verdict: The label lists levothyroxine as a tablet. Most of the dose is taken up in the jejunum and upper ileum, and your small-bowel length is unknown, so it may be absorbed less well than usual.

why.claim: The label says most of the dose is absorbed from the jejunum and upper ileum, which are parts of the small bowel.
The label lists the dosage form as a tablet.
Most oral medicines are absorbed in the first part of the jejunum, so many plain immediate-release medicines can still be absorbed if that part remains.
How well medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma. Your length is unknown.
After bowel surgery, absorption dropped for 29 of 37 medicines studied. The effect differs from drug to drug, so nobody can predict it exactly for one person.
If a medicine doesn't seem to be doing its job, poor absorption could be the reason. Tell your prescriber or pharmacist.
The label I checked had no inactive-ingredient list, so I could not check the fillers in this tablet.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#malabsorption-suspect: If a medicine does not seem to produce its expected effect, malabsorption should be suspected and raised with the prescriber or pharmacist.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

why.claim: Glucotrol XL is an extended-release tablet. It is designed to let the medicine out slowly as it moves through your gut.
Slow-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel to let out their medicine. If your bowel is shorter or food moves through fast, some of the dose may leave your body before it is released.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, guidelines say slow-release and coated medicines are generally avoided.
How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. Your small-bowel length is unknown, so it's hard to say how much this applies to you.
The label says to swallow the tablet whole and not to break, crush, dissolve, chew, or cut it.
The label says the body absorbs all of the medicine (100%), but that was measured in people with type 2 diabetes. It was not measured in people with short bowel.

why.claim: This product is listed as a delayed-release (enteric-coated) tablet.

final.verdict: Depakote is a delayed-release (coated) medicine, and short bowel guidelines say these designs may not fully release the drug when part of the small bowel is gone. That makes it worth checking with your care team.

why.claim: The Depakote label I matched (Depakote Sprinkles) calls it 'divalproex sodium delayed release capsules.' Your entry, 'depakote,' was matched to this form, so check that it is the one on your bottle.
The capsules hold specially coated particles of the medicine.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, delayed-release and coated medicines are usually avoided. They need a long, normal passage through the gut to release the drug.
If food moves through quickly, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some of the medicine can pass through whole.

The label says the capsules can be swallowed whole, or the contents can be sprinkled on soft food and swallowed right away without chewing. It also says the valproate blood level should be checked if the response is not satisfactory.
For medicines where small changes in the amount absorbed matter, doctors may check blood levels or watch the effect closely. That is because absorption after bowel surgery is hard to predict.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. Your length is unknown.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#acid-suppression: Gastric acid hypersecretion is common early after major resection, and acid-suppressing medicines are often used to reduce output; their release form still matters for absorption.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-monitoring: For drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, clinicians may check drug blood levels or watch the clinical effect closely, because absorption after resection is hard to predict.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pd-2017#ors-sodium: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.
evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are used in this patient group, they should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g. , Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Depakote Sprinkle Capsules is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, Depakote Sprinkle Capsules should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with Depakote Sprinkle Capsules for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. In such situations, effective contraception should be used [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 )] . A Medication Guide describing the risks of valproate is available for patients [see Patient Counseling Information ( 17 )] . Pancreatitis Cases of life-threatening pancreatitis have been reported in both children and adults receiving valproate. Some of the cases have been described as hemorrhagic with a rapid progression from initial symptoms to death. Cases have been reported shortly after initial use as well as after several years of use. Patients and guardians should be warned that abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and/or anorexia can be symptoms of pancreatitis that require prompt medical evaluation. If pancreatitis is diagnosed
evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate may not provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of Depakote (divalproex sodium) products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various Depakote and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 ) ] . Distribution Protein Binding The plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent and the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Protein binding of valproate is reduced in the elderly, in patients with chronic hepatic diseases, in patients with renal impairment, and in the presence of other drugs (e.g., aspirin). evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be swallowed whole or the contents may be sprinkled on soft food. The drug/food mixture should be swallowed immediately (avoid chewing) ( 2.2 ) Safety of doses above 60 mg/kg/day is not established ( 2.1 , 2.2 ) Complex Partial Seizures: Start at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response; if response is not satisfactory, check valproate plasma level; see full prescribing information for conversion to monotherapy ( 2.1 ) Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.1 ) 2.1 Epilepsy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are administered orally. As Depakote dosage is titrated upward, concentrations of clonazepam, diazepam, ethosuximide, lamotrigine, tolbutamide, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and/or phenytoin may be affected [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) ] . Complex Partial Seizures For adults and children 10 years of age or older. Monotherapy (Initial Therapy) Depakote Sprinkle Capsules has not been systematically studied as initial therapy. Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. The probability of thrombocytopenia increases significantly at total trough valproate plasma concentrations above 110 mcg/mL in females and 135 mcg/mL in males. The benefit of improved seizure control with higher doses should be weighed against the possibility of a greater incidence of adverse reactions. Conversion to Monotherapy Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50-100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. Concomitant antiepilepsy drug (AED) dosage can ordinarily be reduced by approximately 25% every 2 weeks. This reduction may be started at initiation of Depakote Sprinkle Capsules therapy, or delayed by 1 to 2 weeks if there is a concern that seizures are likely to occur with a reduction. The speed and duration of withdrawal of the concomitant AED can be highly variable, and patients should be monitored closely during this period for increased seizure frequency. Adjunctive Therapy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be added to the patient's regimen at a dosage of 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage may be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. If the total daily dose exceeds 250 mg, it should be given in divided doses. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months of valproate therapy. In progressively older patient groups experience in epilepsy has indicated that the incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably. Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease Depakote Sprinkle Capsules is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 ) ] . draft.verdict: With an end-jejunostomy and no colon, plain water is usually limited because it can make stoma output go up. An oral rehydration solution is usually the preferred drink.

why.claim: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water and other low-salt drinks can pull salt into the gut and raise output. So they are usually limited, and an oral rehydration solution is used instead.
A glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.
It works because the small bowel takes in glucose and salt together, and water comes in with them.
For short bowel syndrome, the solutions usually recommended have about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
The standard WHO solution has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was designed for sudden diarrhea, and that is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
Of 14 people with an end-jejunostomy and no colon who logged plain water, 6 said it made things worse, 4 said it helped, and 4 noticed no change.
Another user with the same anatomy reported that their own dietitian told them plain water can pull salt out and make output worse when there is no colon.

Reported by another user whose small bowel is joined to the colon, from their own care team: people with a colon usually handle water better. This is a different anatomy from yours.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-jejunostomy.text: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-sodium (hypotonic) drinks can pull sodium into the gut and increase output, so these drinks are usually limited in favor of an oral rehydration solution.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#purpose.text: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

final.verdict: With an end-jejunostomy and no colon, plain water is usually limited because it can make stoma output go up. An oral rehydration solution is usually the preferred drink.

why.claim: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water and other low-salt drinks can pull salt into the gut and raise output. So they are usually limited, and an oral rehydration solution is used instead.
A glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.
It works because the small bowel takes in glucose and salt together, and water comes in with them.
For short bowel syndrome, the solutions usually recommended have about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
The standard WHO solution has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was designed for sudden diarrhea, and that is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
Of 14 people with an end-jejunostomy and no colon who logged plain water, 6 said it made things worse, 4 said it helped, and 4 noticed no change.
Another user with the same anatomy reported that their own dietitian told them plain water can pull salt out and make output worse when there is no colon.

draft.ask: ASK: Which rehydration solution or recipe gives me the sodium level used for short bowel with my end-jejunostomy, and is the one I buy strong enough?

careTeamAnswers.summary: Reported by another user with an end-jejunostomy, from their own care team: many store-bought rehydration drinks have less salt than what is used for short bowel. Their dietitian gave them an approved recipe. A clinician endorsed this report.
Reported by another user with an end-jejunostomy, from their own care team: a little lemon or sugar-free flavoring was usually fine, but sorbitol-based flavorings should be avoided.
Reported by another user with an ileostomy, from their own care team: the WHO formula was made for sudden diarrhea, and they needed more salt.

why.claim: A glucose-salt rehydration drink is the preferred drink to replace fluid and salt losses in short bowel, especially with a jejunostomy.
It works because sugar (glucose) and salt (sodium) are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.

With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-salt drinks can pull salt into the gut and raise output. That is why these drinks are usually limited and a rehydration solution is used instead.
For short bowel, guidelines usually suggest a rehydration solution with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

The WHO reduced-osmolarity formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium, 65 chloride, 75 glucose, 20 potassium and 10 citrate. It was designed for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually used for short bowel.
Of 15 people with an end-jejunostomy who logged rehydration solution, 11 said it helped, 3 noticed no change and 1 said it made things worse.
Another user with the same anatomy reported that their own dietitian said many store-bought rehydration drinks are lower in salt than what is used for short bowel. A clinician endorsed this report.

why.claim: A glucose-salt rehydration drink is the preferred drink to replace fluid and salt losses in short bowel, especially with a jejunostomy.
It works because sugar (glucose) and salt (sodium) are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.

With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-salt drinks can pull salt into the gut and raise output. That is why these drinks are usually limited and a rehydration solution is used instead.
For short bowel, guidelines usually suggest a rehydration solution with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

The WHO reduced-osmolarity formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium, 65 chloride, 75 glucose, 20 potassium and 10 citrate. It was designed for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually used for short bowel.
Of 15 people with an end-jejunostomy who logged rehydration solution, 11 said it helped, 3 noticed no change and 1 said it made things worse.
Another user reported that their own dietitian said many store-bought rehydration drinks are lower in salt than what is used for short bowel. This was their care team's advice, not yours.

why.claim: A sugar-and-salt oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink for replacing the fluid and salt lost with short bowel syndrome.
It works because sugar (glucose) and salt are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. You still have 100 to 200 cm of small bowel to do this.
People with an ileostomy are more likely to get dehydrated and low on salt. That is why replacing fluid and salt matters.
For short bowel syndrome, solutions with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium are usually recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

The standard WHO formula has 75 mmol/L sodium, 65 chloride, 75 glucose, 20 potassium and 10 citrate. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually given for short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy logged mixed results: 7 said it helped, 1 saw no change and 6 said it made things worse. That is a reason to ask which strength suits you.
Sugary drinks like juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can increase stoma output, so they are not a good replacement for a proper solution.

draft.verdict: There's nothing in the sources I checked that says coconut water, a hypotonic drink, is a problem for a body with the colon still connected.

why.claim: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is still connected handle ordinary hypotonic drinks better than people with an end-jejunostomy. That's because the colon soaks up water and salt.

Hypertonic, sugary drinks like fruit juice and regular soda can pull water into the gut and make diarrhea worse. Guidelines say to limit those whatever your anatomy. If your coconut water has added sugar or juice, it may be worth checking the label.
When the goal is to replace lost fluid and salt, a glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink in short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, the ORS usually recommended has about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That's more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

draft.verdict: For a colostomy with over 200 cm of small bowel and your colon still connected, I found nothing in the sources I checked against diet soda. I didn't find any guidance on caffeine, though.

why.claim: People whose colon is still connected usually handle ordinary watery drinks better than people with no colon, because the colon takes back water and salt.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the stoma type alone doesn't tell you how much small bowel is left.

Some sugar-free products contain sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, xylitol or mannitol. These pull water into the gut and can make output looser. Most diet sodas don't list them, but it's worth checking the ingredients on the can.
Tell your care team quickly if you get thirsty, have dark or less urine, feel dizzy when you stand up, or your output goes up.

careTeamAnswers.summary: Another user with an ileostomy reported that their own doctor said the WHO formula was made for sudden diarrhea and that they needed more salt.
Another user with an end-jejunostomy reported that their own dietitian said many store-bought ORS products have less sodium than is used for short bowel, and gave them a recipe she approved.
Another user with an end-jejunostomy reported that their own dietitian said a little lemon or sugar-free flavoring is usually fine, but to avoid flavorings made with sorbitol.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask about a short bowel ORS with sodium of about 90 to 120 mmol/L, which is more salt than the WHO formula.

draft.verdict: An oral rehydration drink is the kind of drink advised for short bowel, but the WHO formula has less salt than short bowel sources usually call for, so check with your team before relying on it.

why.claim: A sugar-and-salt oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink for replacing fluid and salt losses in short bowel syndrome.
ORS works because sugar and salt are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.

The WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS has sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel.
For short bowel, ORS with sodium of about 90 to 120 mmol/L is generally recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
Your colon is still connected, and it absorbs water and salt. Because of that, people like you usually handle plain fluids better than people with an end-jejunostomy.
Sports drinks are not a replacement for a short bowel ORS. They are low in salt and high in sugar.
Of 12 people with small bowel joined to colon who logged ORS, 8 said it helped, 2 said no change and 2 said it hurt.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#sports-drinks.text: Typical sports drinks are low in sodium and high in sugar compared with an SBS oral rehydration solution, so they are not a substitute for it.

why.claim: A sugar-and-salt oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink for replacing fluid and salt losses in short bowel syndrome.
ORS works because sugar and salt are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.

The WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS has sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel.
For short bowel, ORS with sodium of about 90 to 120 mmol/L is generally recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
Your colon is still connected, and it absorbs water and salt. Because of that, people like you usually handle plain fluids better than people with an end-jejunostomy.
Sports drinks are not a replacement for a short bowel ORS. They are low in salt and high in sugar.
Of 12 people with small bowel joined to colon who logged ORS, 8 said it helped, 2 said no change and 2 said it hurt.

why.claim: People with short bowel syndrome whose colon is still connected usually handle plain water better than people with an end-jejunostomy. That's because the colon absorbs water and salt.
The advice to limit plain water is aimed at people with an end-jejunostomy and no colon. For them, water can pull salt into the gut and increase output.
Fluid advice is different for each anatomy group, so your team's plan for you still comes first.
Small-bowel length bands show risk. They are not a line above which everything is fine.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and rising output are signs of dehydration. Tell your care team quickly if you notice them.

draft.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked that says to avoid lemonade with your anatomy (a colostomy, more than 200 cm of small bowel, and your colon still connected), but the sources don't address sugary drinks directly.

why.claim: People with short bowel syndrome whose colon is still connected usually handle everyday fluids better than people with an end-jejunostomy. The colon takes back much of the water and salt.
If you choose a sugar-free or 'diet' lemonade, check the label for sorbitol, xylitol or other sugar alcohols. They are poorly absorbed, pull water into the gut, and can increase stoma output.
Lemonade does not replace the salt you lose. When you need to replace fluid and salt, an oral rehydration solution (a salt-and-sugar drink) is the preferred drink.
Tell your care team quickly if you notice thirst, dark urine or less urine than usual, dizziness when you stand up, or more stoma output.

careTeamAnswers.summary: Another user said their own dietitian told them many store-bought rehydration drinks have less salt than what is used for short bowel, and gave them a recipe she approved. That user has no colon. A clinician endorsed this report.
Another user with an ileostomy said their own doctor told them the WHO formula was made for sudden diarrhea and they needed more salt.

draft.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked that says oral rehydration solution won't work for a body with a colostomy, a long small bowel and the colon still connected, but the mix you choose matters.

why.claim: Oral rehydration solution works because sugar (glucose) and salt (sodium) are taken in together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. You still have a long small bowel.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the stoma type alone does not tell you how much small bowel is left.
When the colon is still connected, it takes in water and salt too. So people like you usually handle plain drinks like water better than people with no colon.
Advice on drinks is different for different bowel layouts. Advice written for people with no colon may not fit you.
The WHO formula has sodium 75, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea.
For short bowel syndrome, guidelines usually point to solutions with more sodium, about 90 to 120 mmol/L. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

final.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked that says oral rehydration solution won't work for a body with a colostomy, a long small bowel and the colon still connected, but the mix you choose matters.

why.claim: Oral rehydration solution works because sugar (glucose) and salt (sodium) are taken in together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the stoma type alone does not tell you how much small bowel is left.

When the colon is still connected, it takes in water and salt too. So people with the colon still connected usually handle plain drinks like water better than people with an end-jejunostomy (no colon).
Advice on drinks is different for different bowel layouts. Advice written for people with no colon may not fit you.
The WHO formula has sodium 75, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea.
For short bowel syndrome, guidelines usually point to solutions with more sodium, about 90 to 120 mmol/L. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
Reports from people with a colostomy are mixed: 3 out of 12 said it helped, 4 noticed no change and 5 said it made things worse.

G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups.text: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.

G:aga-sbs#dehydration-signs.text: Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#purpose.text: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

draft.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked that says to avoid mashed potato with an end-jejunostomy, and potatoes are often said to thicken output.

why.claim: Starchy, low-fiber foods like potatoes, white rice, bananas, pasta and plain crackers are often reported to thicken output.

draft.verdict: For an end-jejunostomy with no colon, I found nothing in the sources I checked that says to avoid spinach. The oxalate warning applies mainly when the colon is still connected.

why.claim: The advice to limit high-oxalate foods like spinach is for people whose colon is still connected. In that group, poorly absorbed fat raises oxalate uptake and the risk of kidney stones.
Oxalate effects happen in the colon. With an end-jejunostomy, that limit usually doesn't apply in the same way.
Diet advice is different for each short bowel anatomy group, so spinach advice meant for people with a colon may not fit you.
Another user with an end-jejunostomy said their own dietitian told them oxalate stones are mainly a concern when the colon is still connected.
People with your anatomy reported mixed results: 2 said spinach helped, 8 noticed no change and 3 said it hurt.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-residual-length: Remaining small-bowel length bands (for example under 100 cm with an end-jejunostomy) describe risk of needing nutrition or fluid support; they are risk bands, not a line above which everything is safe.
evidence.G:pd-2017#fat: Fat restriction is mainly useful when the colon is in continuity (because of oxalate and fatty-acid effects in the colon); with an end-jejunostomy, fat is an important energy source and is usually not restricted.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-jejunostomy: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-sodium (hypotonic) drinks can pull sodium into the gut and increase output, so these drinks are usually limited in favor of an oral rehydration solution.
evidence.G:pd-2017#salt: Salting food and choosing salty snacks is commonly encouraged in short bowel syndrome with high output, within the care team's advice for the person's heart and kidney health.
evidence.G:pd-2017#thickening-foods: Starchy, low-fiber foods such as white rice, bananas, potatoes, pasta and plain crackers are often reported to thicken output.

evidence.G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release: The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
