sourcesChecked: Guidelines: AGA SBS update, Practical Gastroenterology #139, Remane 2025, Sood 2013

swapToAskAbout.text: Instead of crushing, ask your pharmacist or doctor whether an immediate-release or liquid form of nifedipine would suit your body. Please don't change anything on your own.

draft.verdict: I can't confirm this. The nifedipine ER label says not to crush these tablets, and SBS guidance says crushing extended-release or coated tablets can be dangerous, so please call a pharmacist (many are open late) before tonight's dose.

why.claim: The label says: do not chew, divide or crush these tablets.
This product is an extended-release tablet.
It has an enteric coating. The coating dissolves as the gut becomes less acidic, and then the drug comes out slowly.
Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous. Crushing is only considered for plain immediate-release tablets, and that is the pharmacist's call.
Guidance for people with a stoma says to talk to a pharmacist before crushing, splitting or switching a medicine.

You're right to be worried about seeing whole tablets. A whole tablet or shell in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left after the drug came out. Show it to your pharmacist. It doesn't prove things either way.
When food moves through fast, an enteric coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
After a large small-bowel resection, slow-release and coated medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal gut to release the drug.
Your colon is not connected. Slow-release products can release part of their dose in the colon, so without it they have less time to work.

swapToAskAbout.text: Au lieu d'écraser le comprimé, demandez si une autre forme de tacrolimus conviendrait mieux à votre corps, par exemple une forme liquide. Les liquides peuvent être mieux absorbés en cas de grêle court, mais ils contiennent souvent des sucres-alcools qui peuvent augmenter ce qui sort par la stomie. Ce choix revient à votre équipe.

draft.verdict: Non : la notice d'Envarsus XR dit clairement de ne pas l'écraser. Votre inquiétude sur l'absorption est réelle, mais la réponse doit venir de votre pharmacien ou de votre équipe de greffe, pas d'un changement fait à la maison.

why.claim: La notice dit d'avaler le comprimé entier avec de l'eau. Il ne faut pas le mâcher, le couper, l'écraser ni le dissoudre.
Envarsus XR est un comprimé à libération prolongée. Il est conçu pour libérer le médicament lentement.
Les guides demandent de parler à un pharmacien avant de changer la forme d'un médicament, par exemple l'écraser, le couper ou changer de produit.
Vous avez raison d'y penser : ce type de comprimé a besoin de temps dans l'intestin. Si le transit est rapide, une partie de la dose peut sortir avant d'être libérée.
Sans côlon relié, les produits à libération lente ont moins de temps et de surface pour libérer le médicament.
Chez les personnes avec une stomie, les formes à libération prolongée sont classées « critiques » pour le risque de mal se dissoudre.
L'absorption dépend surtout de la longueur et de l'état de l'intestin grêle restant. Vous avez plus de 200 cm, et c'est une information utile pour votre équipe.

Selon la notice, Envarsus XR n'est pas absorbé comme les autres formes de tacrolimus : chez des personnes en bonne santé, sa biodisponibilité était environ 50 % plus élevée. Passer d'une forme à une autre n'est donc pas un simple échange.

why.claim: La notice dit d'avaler le comprimé entier avec de l'eau. Il ne faut pas le mâcher, le couper, l'écraser ni le dissoudre.
Envarsus XR est un comprimé à libération prolongée.
Les guides demandent de parler à un pharmacien avant de changer la forme d'un médicament, par exemple l'écraser, le couper ou changer de produit.

Vous avez raison d'y penser : les formes à libération lente ont besoin d'un temps de passage suffisant dans l'intestin grêle. Si le transit est rapide, une partie de la dose peut sortir avant d'être libérée.
Sans côlon, les produits à libération lente ont moins de temps et de surface pour libérer le médicament.
Chez les personnes avec une stomie, les formes à libération prolongée sont classées « critiques » pour le risque de mal se dissoudre.
L'absorption des médicaments dépend surtout de la longueur et de l'état de l'intestin grêle restant, plus que du type de stomie.

Selon la notice, chez des personnes en bonne santé, la biodisponibilité d'Envarsus XR était environ 50 % plus élevée que celle des gélules de tacrolimus à libération immédiate ou prolongée. Passer d'une forme à une autre n'est donc pas un simple échange.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:pd-2017#thickening-foods: Starchy, low-fiber foods such as white rice, bananas, potatoes, pasta and plain crackers are often reported to thicken output.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:remane-2025#patient-education: In the pilot study, 11 of 50 interviewed ostomy patients had seen undissolved medicine, and over 60% said they had not been told how an ostomy can affect their medicines.
evidence.G:remane-2025#tablet-in-pouch: An intact tablet or shell seen in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve, or it can be an empty shell left after the drug was released. It is worth showing the pharmacist; it is not proof either way.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ask-before-changing-form: Patients should consult a pharmacist before changing the dose form of a medicine, such as crushing, splitting or switching products.
evidence.G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release: The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.
evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: Advise patients to swallow ENVARSUS XR tablets whole with fluid (preferably water); patients must not chew, divide, crush or dissovle the tablets.
evidence.L:dosage_forms_and_strengths: Oval, white to off-white uncoated extended-release tablets
evidence.L:pharmacokinetics: In healthy subjects, the oral bioavailability of ENVARSUS XR was approximately 50% higher as compared with both tacrolimus immediate-release and extended-release capsule formulations at steady state.

draft.ask: ASK: My morphine extended-release tablet doesn't seem to work since my colostomy surgery. Am I absorbing it, and would a liquid or immediate-release form suit me better?

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

swapToAskAbout.text: Morphine also comes as a liquid and as an immediate-release form. Guidelines put liquid medicines in the group least likely to have trouble dissolving with an ostomy. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist whether either form would suit you. Don't switch on your own.

draft.verdict: No. The label says to swallow these morphine extended-release tablets whole, so please don't chew them, and tell the doctor who prescribes your pain medicine soon that it doesn't seem to be working.

why.claim: The label tells patients to swallow morphine sulfate extended-release tablets whole.
This is an extended-release tablet, built to let the medicine out slowly over time.
Guidelines say to check with a pharmacist before changing how you take a medicine, such as crushing or switching products.
In people with an ostomy, extended-release products are in the group most likely to have trouble dissolving.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, and medicines are often absorbed normally. But the stoma type alone doesn't prove that.
How well medicines are absorbed depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma.
Even normally, only about 20 to 40% of a morphine dose taken by mouth reaches the body.

why.claim: Pristiq is an extended-release tablet. It is made to let the medicine out slowly.
The label says the tablet must be swallowed whole with fluid. It must not be divided, crushed, chewed, or dissolved.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#acid-suppression: Gastric acid hypersecretion is common early after major resection, and acid-suppressing medicines are often used to reduce output; their release form still matters for absorption.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-monitoring: For drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, clinicians may check drug blood levels or watch the clinical effect closely, because absorption after resection is hard to predict.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release: For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.

evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

why.claim: The label lists this medicine as a plain capsule, not a slow-release form.
The label says almost all of a dose (about 90%) is normally absorbed, and food does not change this much.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain, quick-release medicines can often still be absorbed when that part remains.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel you have left. You have over 200 cm.
Absorption changes differ from drug to drug. So whether this one is working for you should be checked with your prescriber or pharmacist, not guessed.

If you see a capsule or shell in your pouch, it may mean the medicine did not dissolve. It may also be an empty shell left after the drug came out. It's worth showing your pharmacist, but it doesn't prove either one.
People with an ileostomy are more likely to get dehydrated and low on salt. If your output has gone up, tell your team about that too.

evidence.G:hong-2021#drug-specific: Because the change in absorption differs from drug to drug, each medicine should be considered individually with the prescriber or pharmacist.
evidence.G:pd-2017#fat: Fat restriction is mainly useful when the colon is in continuity (because of oxalate and fatty-acid effects in the colon); with an end-jejunostomy, fat is an important energy source and is usually not restricted.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you how many to take. Taking more without your doctor or pharmacist could be risky, but a medicine that isn't giving you relief is a good reason to call them today.

why.claim: This is an extended-release tablet. It is made to let the medicine out slowly over time.
In people with an ostomy, extended-release pills are in the highest-risk group for not dissolving properly.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, and pills are often absorbed normally. But that is not a guarantee.
How well pills absorb depends more on how long and healthy your small bowel is than on the type of stoma.
The label says diclofenac taken by mouth is fully absorbed. But only about half of what is absorbed reaches the bloodstream.
The guidelines say to check with a pharmacist before changing how you take a medicine, for example crushing it, splitting it, or switching products.

If you see whole tablets or shells in your pouch, show the pharmacist. It could mean the tablet didn't dissolve, or it could be an empty shell left after the medicine came out. It doesn't prove either one.

why.claim: After bowel surgery, it is hard to predict how much of a medicine gets absorbed. For some drugs, clinicians may check blood levels or watch closely how well the drug is working, instead of guessing.
This product is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole and not to cut, crush or chew them.

Guidelines say sustained-release medicines are generally avoided after a large part of the small bowel is removed.

final.verdict: I can't give you a yes or no on whether to keep taking torsemide; only your doctor or pharmacist can decide that. why.claim: Your label lists the dosage form as a tablet. It is not listed as extended-release or enteric-coated.
The label says about 80% of each torsemide tablet gets into the body.
Plain tablets that dissolve fast are in the lowest-risk group for people with an ostomy.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain immediate-release medicines can usually still be absorbed when that part is still there.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, so medicines are often absorbed normally. That is likely, but not a guarantee.
The listed inactive ingredients are lactose, microcrystalline cellulose and crospovidone. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohols are listed.
Tell your care team quickly if you notice thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, or rising stoma output. These are warning signs of dehydration.

why.claim: METADATE CD is an extended-release capsule.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, slow-release and coated medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. You have under 100 cm.
The label says not to crush or chew the capsule or what is inside it. So opening it is not a workaround to try on your own.
I can't let a doctor's okay that I haven't seen override a guideline. But your doctor may know things about your gut that I don't, like how fast it moves. A quick check with them settles it.

draft.verdict: I can't call any medicine "safe." Your GI doctor's okay counts for a lot because they know your body, and with a colostomy most of the small bowel is usually still there. But this is an enteric-coated tablet, and that type is worth one quick check with your pharmacist.

why.claim: Your tablet is a delayed-release tablet.
The label says the tablets are pink, oval and enteric-coated.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole and not crush or chew them.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, so pills are often absorbed normally. Still, the type of stoma alone does not guarantee it.
How well pills are absorbed depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma. You have over 200 cm, which your doctor would have kept in mind.
Most pills are absorbed in the upper small bowel.
A study of people with an ostomy put enteric-coated and extended-release products in the highest-risk group for not dissolving properly.
In that study, 11 of 50 people with an ostomy had seen undissolved medicine. Over 60% said nobody had told them how an ostomy can affect their medicines.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS See full prescribing information for complete boxed warning. Hepatotoxicity, including fatalities, usually during the first 6 months of treatment. Children under the age of two years and patients with mitochondrial disorders are at higher risk. Monitor patients closely, and perform serum liver testing prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter ( 5.1 ) Fetal Risk, particularly neural tube defects, other major malformations, and decreased IQ ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 ) Pancreatitis, including fatal hemorrhagic cases ( 5.5 ) Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g., Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Divalproex sodium is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, divalproex sodium should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with divalproex sodium for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate cannot provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. Mania In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to clinical response with trough plasma concentrations between 50 and 125 mcg/mL [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 )]. 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of divalproex sodium products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Whether or not rate of absorption influences the efficacy of valproate as an antimanic or antimigraine agent is unknown. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various divalproex sodium and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 )] . Nonetheless, any changes in dosage administration, or the addition or discontinuance of concomitant drugs should ordinarily be accompanied by close monitoring of clinical status and valproate plasma concentrations. evidence.L:description: 11 DESCRIPTION Divalproex sodium is a stable co-ordination compound comprised of sodium valproate and valproic acid in a 1:1 molar relationship and formed during the partial neutralization of valproic acid with 0.5 equivalent of sodium hydroxide. Chemically it is designated as sodium hydrogen bis(2-propylpentanoate). Divalproex sodium has the following structure: Divalproex sodium occurs as a white powder with a characteristic odor. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP are for oral administration. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP are supplied in three dosage strengths containing divalproex sodium equivalent to 125 mg, 250 mg, or 500 mg of valproic acid. Inactive Ingredients Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP: colloidal silicon dioxide, D&C Red No. 30, FD&C Blue No. 2, hydroxylpropyl cellulose, hypromellose, hypromellose phthalate, iron oxide black, iron oxide yellow, low substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, pregelatinised starch, propylene glycol, shellac, talc, titanium dioxide, triethyl citrate. evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are administered orally in divided doses. The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.2 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Migraine: The recommended starting dose is 250 mg twice daily, thereafter increasing to a maximum of 1,000 mg/day as needed ( 2.3 ). Patients should be informed to take divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets every day as prescribed. If a dose is missed it should be taken as soon as possible, unless it is almost time for the next dose. If a dose is skipped, the patient should not double the next dose. 2.1 Mania Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are administered orally. The recommended initial dose is 750 mg daily in divided doses. The dose should be increased as rapidly as possible to achieve the lowest therapeutic dose which produces the desired clinical effect or the desired range of plasma concentrations. In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to a clinical response with a trough plasma concentration between 50 and 125 mcg/mL. Maximum concentrations were generally achieved within 14 days. The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day. Conversely, valproate may displace certain protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, and tolbutamide) [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) for more detailed information on the pharmacokinetic interactions of valproate with other drugs]. CNS Distribution: Valproate concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) approximate unbound concentrations in plasma (about 10% of total concentration). Metabolism Valproate is metabolized almost entirely by the liver. In adult patients on monotherapy, 30 to 50% of an administered dose appears in urine as a glucuronide conjugate. Mitochondrial β-oxidation is the other major metabolic pathway, typically accounting for over 40% of the dose. Usually, less than 15 to 20% of the dose is eliminated by other oxidative mechanisms. Less than 3% of an administered dose is excreted unchanged in urine. The relationship between dose and total valproate concentration is nonlinear; concentration does not increase proportionally with the dose, but rather, increases to a lesser extent due to saturable plasma protein binding. The kinetics of unbound drug are linear. Elimination Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for total valproate are 0.56 L/hr/1.73 m 2 and 11 L/1.73 m 2 , respectively. Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for free valproate are 4.6 L/hr

evidence.L:warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Birth defects, decreased IQ, and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure: Should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant or to treat a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 ) Pancreatitis: Divalproex sodium should ordinarily be discontinued ( 5.5 ) Suicidal behavior or ideation: Antiepileptic drugs, including divalproex sodium, increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior ( 5.7 ) Bleeding and other hematopoietic disorders: Monitor platelet counts and coagulation tests ( 5.8 ) Hyperammonemia and hyperammonemic encephalopathy: Measure ammonia level if unexplained lethargy and vomiting or changes in mental status, and also with concomitant topiramate use; consider discontinuation of valproate therapy ( 5.6 , 5.9 , 5.10 ) Hypothermia: Hypothermia has been reported during valproate therapy with occur in patients using concomitant topiramate ( 5.11 ) Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)/Multiorgan Hypersensitivity Reaction; serious dermatologic reactions, and angioedema: Discontinue divalproex sodium unless an alternate etiology is established ( 4 , 5.12 , 5.13 , 5.14 ) 5.1 Hepatotoxicity General Information on Hepatotoxicity Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months of valproate therapy. However, healthcare providers should not rely totally on serum biochemistry since these tests may not be abnormal in all instances, but should also consider the results of careful interim medical history and physical examination. Caution should be observed when administering valproate products to patients with a prior history of hepatic disease. Patients on multiple anticonvulsants, children, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease may be at particular risk. See below, "Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease." Experience has indicated that children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those with the aforementioned conditions. When divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. In progressively older patient groups experience in epilepsy has indicated that the incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably. Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease Divalproex sodium is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )]. Valproate-induced acute liver failure and liver-related deaths have been reported in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by mutations in the gene for mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ (POLG) (e.g., Alpers-Huttenlocher Syndrome) at a higher rate than those without these syndromes. Most of the reported cases of liver failure in patients with these syndromes have been identified in children and adolescents. swapToAskAbout.text: Guidelines say it's often worth asking the pharmacist about an immediate-release or liquid version of the same medicine. Liquids can be absorbed more reliably, but many contain sugar alcohols that can increase output, so ask about those too.

draft.verdict: I can't mark this green or call it safe, because short bowel guidelines say extended-release and enteric-coated tablets like this one are generally avoided. Your urologist knows you best, though, so the next step is to bring this exact concern back to them or your pharmacist.

why.claim: The product is listed as an extended-release tablet.
The label says it has an enteric coat that does not dissolve in stomach acid. That means it is built to travel further down the gut before it releases the medicine.
The label says the tablet must be swallowed whole and must not be chewed, divided, or crushed.

After a large part of the small bowel has been removed, guidelines say slow-release and enteric-coated medicines are generally avoided. They count on a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
When the gut is shorter or moves things faster, some of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
With fast transit, an enteric coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.

Your profile says you have under 100 cm of small bowel joined to your colon. That kind of shortened gut is what these guidelines describe. A urologist may not have been thinking about how this tablet releases its medicine in a short gut, so it's worth asking about directly.

draft.ask: ASK: Tenho jejunostomia terminal, menos de 100 cm de intestino e sem cólon. Como saberemos se a quetiapina de liberação prolongada está sendo bem absorvida no meu caso?

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

swapToAskAbout.text: Se você e seu médico quiserem, perguntar se uma versão de liberação imediata ou líquida da quetiapina faria sentido para você. Não mude nada por conta própria.

draft.verdict: Não posso marcar como verde: a decisão do seu médico vale e não peço que você mude nada, mas as diretrizes ainda apontam um risco de absorção da quetiapina de liberação prolongada no seu tipo de intestino, e isso vale a pena confirmar com ele ou com o farmacêutico.

why.claim: Este produto é um comprimido de liberação prolongada.
O rótulo diz que o comprimido deve ser engolido inteiro, sem partir, mastigar ou triturar.
Depois de uma grande retirada do intestino delgado, remédios de liberação lenta costumam ser evitados, porque precisam de um trânsito longo e normal para soltar o remédio.
Com o intestino mais curto ou trânsito rápido, parte da dose pode sair do corpo antes de ser liberada.
Sem cólon, produtos de liberação lenta têm menos tempo e menos superfície para liberar o remédio.
Um estudo com pessoas com estomia coloca os produtos de liberação prolongada no grupo de maior risco de não se dissolverem.
Seu médico conhece seu caso e pode ter motivos para essa escolha. Esse aviso não é uma ordem para parar: é algo para conversar e acompanhar com ele.

evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release: The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

draft.verdict: I can't call Depakote "safe" or mark it green, but your doctor's okay matters a lot, so keep taking it as prescribed. The one thing worth checking is that Depakote comes in a delayed-release form, and short bowel guidelines flag that form.

why.claim: The label I read is for Depakote Sprinkle Capsules. The label calls them delayed-release capsules.
The capsules hold specially coated particles of the medicine.
After a lot of small bowel has been removed, delayed-release and coated medicines are usually avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to let the drug out.
If things move through your gut fast, the coating may not dissolve in time.
How well pills get absorbed depends mostly on how long and healthy your remaining small bowel is. We don't know your length, so this may matter a lot for you or very little.
For medicines like this, where the right amount in the blood matters, doctors can check a blood level, because absorption after bowel surgery is hard to predict.
The Depakote label also says a blood level can be checked if the medicine isn't working well enough.

evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release: For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.

evidence.G:pg139#extended-release-avoid: Extended-release products are generally avoided after extensive resection; an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often a question worth asking the pharmacist about.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are used in this patient group, they should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g. , Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Depakote Sprinkle Capsules is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, Depakote Sprinkle Capsules should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with Depakote Sprinkle Capsules for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. In such situations, effective contraception should be used [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 )] . A Medication Guide describing the risks of valproate is available for patients [see Patient Counseling Information ( 17 )] . Pancreatitis Cases of life-threatening pancreatitis have been reported in both children and adults receiving valproate. Some of the cases have been described as hemorrhagic with a rapid progression from initial symptoms to death. Cases have been reported shortly after initial use as well as after several years of use. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate may not provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of Depakote (divalproex sodium) products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various Depakote and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 ) ] . Distribution Protein Binding The plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent and the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Protein binding of valproate is reduced in the elderly, in patients with chronic hepatic diseases, in patients with renal impairment, and in the presence of other drugs (e.g., aspirin). evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be swallowed whole or the contents may be sprinkled on soft food. The drug/food mixture should be swallowed immediately (avoid chewing) ( 2.2 ) Safety of doses above 60 mg/kg/day is not established ( 2.1 , 2.2 ) Complex Partial Seizures: Start at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response; if response is not satisfactory, check valproate plasma level; see full prescribing information for conversion to monotherapy ( 2.1 ) Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.1 ) 2.1 Epilepsy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are administered orally. As Depakote dosage is titrated upward, concentrations of clonazepam, diazepam, ethosuximide, lamotrigine, tolbutamide, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and/or phenytoin may be affected [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) ] . Complex Partial Seizures For adults and children 10 years of age or older. Monotherapy (Initial Therapy) Depakote Sprinkle Capsules has not been systematically studied as initial therapy. Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. The probability of thrombocytopenia increases significantly at total trough valproate plasma concentrations above 110 mcg/mL in females and 135 mcg/mL in males. The benefit of improved seizure control with higher doses should be weighed against the possibility of a greater incidence of adverse reactions. Conversion to Monotherapy Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50-100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. Concomitant antiepilepsy drug (AED) dosage can ordinarily be reduced by approximately 25% every 2 weeks. This reduction may be started at initiation of Depakote Sprinkle Capsules therapy, or delayed by 1 to 2 weeks if there is a concern that seizures are likely to occur with a reduction. The speed and duration of withdrawal of the concomitant AED can be highly variable, and patients should be monitored closely during this period for increased seizure frequency. Adjunctive Therapy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be added to the patient's regimen at a dosage of 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage may be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. If the total daily dose exceeds 250 mg, it should be given in divided doses. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months of valproate therapy. Caution should be observed when administering valproate products to patients with a prior history of hepatic disease. See below, “Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease.” Experience has indicated that children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those with the aforementioned conditions. When Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. In progressively older patient groups experience in epilepsy has indicated that the incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably. Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease Depakote Sprinkle Capsules is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 ) ] . Valproate-induced acute liver failure and liver-related deaths have been reported in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by mutations in the gene for mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ (POLG) (e.g., Alpers-Huttenlocher Syndrome) at a higher rate than those without these syndromes. why.claim: This medicine is a liquid (a solution), not an extended-release or coated tablet.
Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome. But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols, which can raise stoma output.

Concentrated simple sugars draw water into the bowel and are usually limited in short bowel syndrome. Fructose is a simple sugar, so it is worth watching your output.

draft.ask: ASK: My aspirin is coated, and I have short bowel with my colon still connected. Is it being absorbed, and would a plain uncoated form work better for me?

diagram.label: Timed-release and coated designs expect a long intestine; a shorter gut gives them less time

sourcesChecked: FDA label: description, clinical_pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, how_supplied (absent)

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask whether a plain (immediate-release) aspirin would suit your gut better than a coated one, if aspirin is still right for you.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you to stop or keep taking your aspirin, or what dose to take. That isn't a rule I can switch off. What I can say is that a coated, delayed-release aspirin may not dissolve in time in a shorter gut, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: After a lot of small bowel has been removed, guidelines generally avoid delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines. These designs count on a long, normal trip through the gut to let the drug out.
Coated tablets are made to get past the stomach before they dissolve. When things move through quickly, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
The only label I could match is a plain aspirin tablet, not a coated one. So I couldn't confirm the coating of the aspirin you actually take, and most of that label's sections were missing.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. If that part is still there, many plain (not coated) tablets can still be absorbed.
Crushing a coated tablet defeats its design and can be dangerous. Whether a tablet can be crushed is a decision for the pharmacist.

final.verdict: I can't tell you to stop or keep taking your aspirin, or what dose to take. That isn't a rule I can switch off. What I can say is that a coated, delayed-release aspirin may not dissolve in time in a shorter gut, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: After a lot of small bowel has been removed, guidelines generally avoid delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines. These designs count on a long, normal trip through the gut to let the drug out.
Coated tablets are made to get past the stomach before they dissolve. When things move through quickly, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.

The only label I could match lists the form only as 'tablet'. It doesn't say whether it is coated, so I couldn't confirm the coating of the aspirin you actually take, and most of that label's sections were missing.

draft.verdict: I can't give you an amount to swallow or tell you to swallow Peridex. I follow the same rules as before, and the Peridex label I found has no directions section, so please check the instructions on your bottle or ask your pharmacist or dentist.

why.claim: The Peridex label lists it as a rinse, which is a liquid.
The Peridex ingredient list shows chlorhexidine gluconate and glycerin. It does not list sorbitol, xylitol or mannitol.
A generic 0.12% chlorhexidine rinse label says chlorhexidine is poorly absorbed from the gut. So swallowing it is not a way to get the medicine into your body.

Guidelines say sugar alcohols in liquid medicines are poorly absorbed, pull water into the gut, and can raise stoma output. With an end-jejunostomy, it's worth asking whether the glycerin matters if any rinse is swallowed.
Guidelines also say liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can raise output.

draft.ask: ASK: I feel fine and like lemonade. With my ileostomy, how much sugary drink is okay for me, and should I be drinking an oral rehydration solution instead?

diagram.label: Fluid and salt balance is set in the small bowel

sourcesChecked: Guidelines: hypertonic sugary drinks, simple sugars, sports drinks, dehydration signs, ileostomy dehydration, ORS

swapToAskAbout.text: An oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the drink the guidelines prefer for replacing fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome. For short bowel syndrome, the guidelines usually cite a sodium level of about 90 to 120 mmol/L. That is higher than many store-bought rehydration drinks. Ask your team which one fits you.

draft.verdict: I can't agree with this one. Lemonade is a sugary drink, not just water with lemon, and the guidelines say to limit drinks like it with an ileostomy, even when you feel fine.

why.claim: Sweet drinks like juice and regular soda pull water into the gut. That can raise stoma output, so the guidelines say to limit them whatever your anatomy. The sugar is what makes lemonade different from water.
Sweetened drinks are high in simple sugar. That kind of sugar draws water into the bowel, so it is generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of drying out and of low sodium (salt), so feeling fine today doesn't rule it out.
Warning signs to watch for: thirst, dark urine or peeing less, feeling dizzy when you stand up, and a rise in stoma output. If you notice any of these, tell your care team soon.
What actually helps you hydrate is salt and sugar together, in the right balance. Lemonade has the sugar but not the salt. An oral rehydration solution (ORS) has both.

Drinks are usually sipped through the day rather than taken in large amounts at once.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you to drink as much Gatorade as you like: with short bowel syndrome, guidelines say sports drinks have too little salt and too much sugar to replace an oral rehydration solution (ORS), so how much fluid to drink, and which kind, is a question for your care team.

why.claim: Sports drinks are made for athletes, not for short bowel. Typical sports drinks have little salt and lots of sugar compared with an ORS made for short bowel syndrome, so they can't replace it.
For short bowel syndrome, a sugar-and-salt ORS is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt.
ORS drinks for short bowel syndrome usually have about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. Many store-bought rehydration drinks have less than that.

ORS works because salt and sugar are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. Getting the balance right matters, so more of a drink with the wrong balance is not the same as better hydration.

In your favor: your colon is still connected, and it absorbs water and salt. Most people with short bowel syndrome and a connected colon handle ordinary fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy.
Having a longer length of small bowel lowers your risk, but it does not mean everything is fine past a certain length.
Of 10 people with a colostomy who logged sports drinks, 1 said they helped, 6 noticed no change and 3 said they made things worse.
Watch for signs of dehydration: thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and more output than usual. Tell your care team quickly if you notice any of them.

draft.verdict: Not quite. Tea is mostly water, but it has caffeine, and guidelines say caffeine can raise output and fluid loss. They do not say that more tea is healthier, so drinking a lot of tea every day is worth checking with your team.

why.claim: Your colon is still connected, and it soaks up water and salt. That is why people like you usually handle plain low-salt drinks better than people without a colon.
But tea has caffeine. Caffeine can increase output and fluid loss, so it is usually limited in short bowel syndrome. That means caffeinated tea may not hydrate you the way plain water would.
Guidelines suggest sipping drinks through the day, not drinking a lot at once. Many teams also suggest drinking apart from meals.
Sugar or syrup in tea pulls water into the bowel. Sweetened drinks are generally limited.
Tell your team soon if you get thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, or rising output. These are warning signs of dehydration.
Out of 16 people with your anatomy who logged tea, 4 said it helped, 10 noticed no change, and 2 said it hurt. These are personal reports, not proof.

final.verdict: I can't say drinking orange juice all day is OK: with an ileostomy, more is not better here, because the guidelines say to limit sugary drinks like juice since they can raise stoma output.

why.claim: Fruit juice is a sugary drink that is more concentrated than your body fluids. It pulls water into the gut and can raise stoma output. The guideline says to limit it, whatever your anatomy.
Concentrated sugars, including sweetened drinks, draw water into the bowel. They are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy already have a higher risk of losing too much water and salt.
Guidelines say an oral rehydration solution (ORS), which has both sugar and salt, is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt.
For short bowel syndrome, the ORS usually recommended has about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more than many store-bought drinks have.
Guidelines also suggest sipping drinks slowly through the day instead of drinking a lot at once.
Of 13 people with an ileostomy who logged orange juice, 6 said it hurt, 6 noticed no change and 1 said it helped. These are self-reports and include some sample data.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask about an oral rehydration solution (ORS) made for short bowel syndrome. Guidelines say it is the best drink for replacing fluid and salt with a jejunostomy. Salt and sugar taken in together help your small bowel absorb water. The standard WHO formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium, which is below the range usually given for short bowel syndrome. So ask which one fits you.

draft.verdict: No. Guidelines say to limit sugary, caffeinated drinks like Red Bull with an end-jejunostomy, because they can raise your stoma output and make you lose more fluid. Being this tired can also be a sign of dehydration, so please call your care team today.

why.claim: Sugary drinks pull water into the gut. They can raise stoma output, so guidelines say to limit them.
Sweetened drinks draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
Caffeine can increase output and fluid loss. It is usually limited in short bowel syndrome. Red Bull may feel like it keeps you going, but it can work against your fluid balance.
With an end-jejunostomy, low-salt drinks can pull salt into your gut and raise output.

A drink that says it has "electrolytes" may still not have enough salt. For short bowel syndrome, the rehydration drinks usually recommended have about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more than many store-bought drinks have.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, feeling dizzy when you stand, and more stoma output are warning signs of dehydration. Tell your care team about them right away.

swapToAskAbout.text: One user posted a swap from coffee to an oral rehydration solution (ORS). Nobody with your anatomy posted it, and no clinician has endorsed it, but it passed a guideline check. Guidelines name ORS as the preferred drink for replacing fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome. Ask your team which ORS fits you.

draft.verdict: No. Guidelines don't support unlimited cups: black coffee has no sugar, but its caffeine can raise your output and make you lose more fluid, so it is usually limited in short bowel syndrome.

why.claim: "No sugar" doesn't mean no concern. The caffeine is the issue. Caffeine can raise output and fluid losses, and it is usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
"It's a liquid, so it hydrates" isn't the whole story. A drink that raises output can make you lose fluid as well as take it in.

Your colon is still connected, and that helps. Most people with your setup handle plain drinks like water better than people without a colon, because the colon takes back water and salt. That benefit is for plain drinks like water. It doesn't cancel out the caffeine.
Guidelines suggest sipping drinks slowly through the day, not having a lot at once. Many teams also suggest having drinks apart from meals. Cup after cup goes against this.
Watch for signs of dehydration: thirst, dark urine or peeing less, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or more output. Tell your care team quickly if these happen.
Guidelines name a glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution (ORS) as the preferred drink to replace fluid and salt losses in short bowel syndrome.
Of 13 people with your anatomy who logged coffee, 4 said it hurt, 6 noticed no change and 3 said it helped.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask about an oral rehydration solution as your main drink. It works because salt and sugar together help your gut take in water. For short bowel syndrome, it needs more salt than the WHO formula or most store-bought drinks have. Ask your team which one is right for you, and whether some sweet tea can still fit in your day.

draft.verdict: I know sweet tea is a big part of your life, and I'm not trying to take it away. But with an end-jejunostomy, the guidelines say it doesn't hydrate you the way it seems to, and they usually say to limit it, not drink as much as you want.

why.claim: Without a colon, the jejunum you have left controls your fluid balance. Low-salt drinks like tea can pull salt out of your body into the gut, which raises output. So tea can leave you with less fluid, not more. That's why these drinks are usually limited and an oral rehydration solution is used instead.
The sugar matters too. Sweetened drinks pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
Tea also has caffeine, which can raise output and fluid loss. It is usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
Guidelines suggest sipping drinks slowly through the day instead of drinking a lot at once. Many care teams also suggest keeping drinks apart from meals.
Watch for thirst, dark urine or less urine, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or output going up. These are signs of dehydration. Call your care team quickly if you notice them.

draft.verdict: I can't give you a number of packets. How much ORS you need depends on how much fluid and salt you lose, and only your care team can set that amount for your body.

why.claim: An oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy. The guideline doesn't give one daily amount that fits everyone.
With an end-jejunostomy and no colon, your remaining jejunum controls how much fluid you hold on to. Low-salt drinks like plain water, tea and coffee can actually raise your output.

For short bowel, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium is usually recommended. That's more salt than many store-bought drinks have. I can't confirm DripDrop is in that range, so the right drink matters as much as how much you have.
Watch for thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and rising stoma output. These are warning signs of dehydration. Tell your care team quickly if you notice them.

Of 15 people with an end-jejunostomy who logged an oral rehydration solution, 11 said it helped, 3 said it made no difference and 1 said it made things worse. This is self-reported and includes some made-up sample data.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask your dietitian for an ORS recipe they have checked, with sodium in the short bowel range (about 90 to 120 mmol/L), and how much of it to sip each day.

draft.verdict: I can't give you an amount per day or a salt-and-sugar recipe. Those need to come from your own team, and the WHO formula has less salt than short bowel sources usually recommend.

why.claim: WHO ORS has sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea. Its sodium is lower than the range usually given for short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L sodium is generally recommended. So copying the WHO recipe at home may give you less salt than your body needs.
ORS only works when the sugar and salt are in balance, because they are taken up together and pull water in with them. A mix that is off in either direction may not work as well.
Drinks with too much sugar pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output. That is one reason a homemade mix should follow a recipe your team has checked.
Sources don't give one amount for everyone. They say to sip drinks slowly through the day instead of drinking a lot at once, and many teams suggest keeping drinks apart from meals.
People with an ileostomy have a higher risk of dehydration and low sodium.
Tell your team quickly if you notice thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, or your stoma output going up.
Results were mixed among people with an ileostomy who logged ORS: 7 said it helped, 1 saw no change, and 6 said it made things worse.
Another user (end-jejunostomy) said their own dietitian gave them a recipe she had approved, because many store-bought ORS products are low in sodium for short bowel.

Your profile says your small bowel is joined to your colon, but you said you have an ileostomy. The advice on fluids depends on whether your colon is still connected, so please update your profile and tell your team which one is right.
An oral rehydration drink with glucose and salt is the preferred way to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, the usual sodium level is about 90 to 120 mmol/L, and many store-bought rehydration drinks have less. I could not confirm how much sodium DripDrop has.
Fluids are usually sipped through the day instead of drunk in big amounts at once. Many teams also suggest keeping drinks separate from meals.
Sugary drinks like juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can make output go up.
With an ileostomy, 7 of 14 people said oral rehydration solution helped, 6 said it hurt, and 1 noticed no difference.

draft.ask: ASK: My stoma output is watery. How much rehydration drink should I have each day, is Pedialyte salty enough, and which warning signs mean I should call you?

careTeamAnswers.summary: Another user reported that their own dietitian said many store-bought rehydration drinks have less salt than is used for short bowel. The dietitian gave them a recipe she approved.
Another user reported that their own doctor said the WHO formula was made for sudden diarrhea, and that they needed more salt.
Another user reported that their own dietitian said a little lemon or sugar-free flavoring is usually fine in a rehydration drink. The dietitian said to avoid flavorings made with sorbitol.

draft.verdict: I can't give you an exact number of ounces. That amount has to come from your own care team, and watery stoma output is a warning sign you should tell them about soon.

why.claim: Watery output going up is a warning sign of dehydration. So are thirst, dark urine or peeing less, and feeling dizzy when you stand up. The guidelines say to tell your care team about these signs soon.
A rehydration drink with both sugar and salt is the preferred drink for short bowel. It replaces the water and salt you lose.

For short bowel, the guidelines usually recommend a rehydration drink with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. Many store-bought drinks have less salt than that. So the right drink and the right amount are both questions for your team.
The WHO standard formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and that is below the range usually given for short bowel.

Your profile says your colon is still connected. But you mentioned a stoma. Fluid advice is different for people with a stoma and for people with a connected colon. Please tell your team exactly what you have, and update your profile too.
Sugary drinks like juice and regular soda can make output higher. The guidelines say to limit them.
Of 12 people with your type of bowel who logged a rehydration drink, 8 said it helped, 2 said no change and 2 said it made things worse.

G:aga-sbs#dehydration-signs.text: Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic.text: Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask your dietitian for a home ORS recipe with more salt, in the 90 to 120 mmol/L sodium range cited for short bowel syndrome, measured with spoons you have at home.

draft.verdict: I can't give teaspoon or tablespoon amounts. Also, the WHO recipe itself has less salt than the level usually cited for short bowel syndrome, so the best person to give you a home recipe is your dietitian, who can match it to your body.

why.claim: A drink made with glucose and salt (ORS) is the preferred way to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.
ORS works because sugar and salt are absorbed together in the small bowel and pull water in with them. So the balance between them matters.

The WHO formula contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium is usually recommended. That is more than the WHO formula and many store-bought drinks have.
Sports drinks don't work as a replacement. They are low in salt and high in sugar compared with short bowel ORS.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium. So it matters that your drink has the right amount of salt.
People with an ileostomy who logged ORS had mixed results: 7 said it helped, 1 saw no change, and 6 said it made things worse. Some of these logs are sample data.

careTeamAnswers.summary: Rapport\u00e9 par un autre utilisateur (j\u00e9junostomie, sans c\u00f4lon), d'apr\u00e8s sa propre \u00e9quipe de soins : son di\u00e9t\u00e9ticien a dit que beaucoup de SRO du commerce contiennent moins de sodium que ce qu'on utilise dans le gr\u00eale court, et lui a donn\u00e9 une recette valid\u00e9e. Approuv\u00e9 par un clinicien.

Rapport\u00e9 par un autre utilisateur (il\u00e9ostomie), d'apr\u00e8s sa propre \u00e9quipe de soins : son m\u00e9decin a dit que la formule de l'OMS avait \u00e9t\u00e9 faite pour la diarrh\u00e9e aigu\u00eb et qu'il lui fallait plus de sel.

swapToAskAbout.text: Demandez si une SRO \u00e0 environ 90 \u00e0 120 mmol/L de sodium vous conviendrait mieux que le Pedialyte, et combien en boire.

draft.verdict: Je ne peux pas vous donner de quantité par jour : elle doit être fixée par votre équipe de soins. Et comme votre stomie coule beaucoup, c'est un signal d'alerte à signaler rapidement.

why.claim: Un d\u00e9bit de stomie qui augmente fait partie des signes de d\u00e9shydratation, avec la soif, des urines fonc\u00e9es ou rares et des vertiges en se levant. Il faut en parler vite \u00e0 l'\u00e9quipe de soins.
Une solution de r\u00e9hydratation orale (SRO) avec du sucre et du sel reste la boisson pr\u00e9f\u00e9r\u00e9e pour remplacer l'eau et le sel perdus, surtout avec une j\u00e9junostomie.

Dans le syndrome du gr\u00eale court, on conseille en g\u00e9n\u00e9ral une SRO \u00e0 environ 90 \u00e0 120 mmol/L de sodium. C'est plus que dans beaucoup de boissons de r\u00e9hydratation du commerce. Je ne peux pas confirmer que le Pedialyte atteint ce niveau.
M\u00eame la SRO de l'OMS (sodium 75 mmol/L) a \u00e9t\u00e9 con\u00e7ue pour la diarrh\u00e9e aigu\u00eb. Son sodium est en dessous de la plage habituelle du gr\u00eale court.
Avec une j\u00e9junostomie terminale, les boissons pauvres en sel (eau, th\u00e9, caf\u00e9) peuvent augmenter le d\u00e9bit. On les limite donc en g\u00e9n\u00e9ral au profit d'une SRO.

Votre profil indique une j\u00e9junostomie terminale sans c\u00f4lon, mais vous parlez d'une il\u00e9ostomie. Les retours de la communaut\u00e9 diff\u00e8rent selon l'anatomie : 11 personnes sur 15 avec une j\u00e9junostomie terminale disent que la SRO les a aid\u00e9es, contre 7 sur 14 avec une il\u00e9ostomie (6 ont eu un probl\u00e8me). V\u00e9rifiez votre type de stomie avec votre \u00e9quipe.

Rapporté par un autre utilisateur, d'après sa propre équipe de soins (pas la vôtre) : son médecin a dit que la formule de l'OMS avait été faite pour la diarrhée aiguë et qu'il lui fallait plus de sel.

G:aga-sbs#dehydration-signs.text: Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-jejunostomy.text: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-sodium (hypotonic) drinks can pull sodium into the gut and increase output, so these drinks are usually limited in favor of an oral rehydration solution.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

final.verdict: Je ne peux pas vous donner de quantité par jour : elle doit être fixée par votre équipe de soins. Et comme votre stomie coule beaucoup, c'est un signal d'alerte à signaler rapidement.

why.claim: Un débit de stomie qui augmente fait partie des signes de déshydratation, avec la soif, des urines foncées ou rares et des vertiges en se levant. Il faut en parler vite à l'équipe de soins.
Une solution de réhydratation orale (SRO) avec du sucre et du sel reste la boisson préférée pour remplacer l'eau et le sel perdus, surtout avec une jéjunostomie.

Dans le syndrome du grêle court, on conseille en général une SRO à environ 90 à 120 mmol/L de sodium. C'est plus que dans beaucoup de boissons de réhydratation du commerce. Je ne peux pas confirmer que le Pedialyte atteint ce niveau.
Même la SRO de l'OMS (sodium 75 mmol/L) a été conçue pour la diarrhée aiguë. Son sodium est en dessous de la plage habituelle du grêle court.
Avec une jéjunostomie terminale, les boissons pauvres en sel (eau, thé, café) peuvent augmenter le débit. On les limite donc en général au profit d'une SRO.

Votre profil indique une jéjunostomie terminale sans côlon, mais vous parlez d'une iléostomie. Les retours de la communauté diffèrent selon l'anatomie : 11 personnes sur 15 avec une jéjunostomie terminale disent que la SRO les a aidées, contre 7 sur 14 avec une iléostomie (6 ont eu un problème). Vérifiez votre type de stomie avec votre équipe.
