draft.verdict: Seeing Horizant in your pouch is a real concern to show your pharmacist today, but it does not prove the medicine isn't working, and stopping it or switching to another version is a decision to make with your pharmacist or prescriber, not on your own.

why.claim: A whole tablet or shell in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left behind after the medicine came out. It's worth showing the pharmacist, but it doesn't prove things either way.
You're not alone. In one study, 11 of 50 people with an ostomy had seen medicine that hadn't dissolved.
Horizant is made as an extended-release (slow-release) tablet.
The label says to swallow it whole and not cut, crush or chew it.
Crushing extended-release products ruins how they're designed to work and can be dangerous.
After a lot of small bowel has been removed, slow-release medicines are generally avoided, because they need a long, normal trip through the gut to let the medicine out.
When the bowel is short or things move through fast, part of the dose may leave the body before it's released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the colon. With no colon, they have less time and less gut to work with.

The label says about 75% of the dose is taken up when taken with food. The label sections I had don't say whether that holds for someone without a colon. The section that usually describes what the tablet looks like wasn't available, so I can't match what you saw to the label.

G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release.text: For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.

draft.ask: ASK: I'm seeing carbamazepine ER bits in my ileostomy bag. I brought some. Can you check whether I'm absorbing it, and whether I should switch forms, and how to do that safely?

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

sourcesChecked: Guidelines: extended-release absorption with an ileostomy

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask your prescriber and pharmacist whether a form that isn't extended-release would suit your body better. Also ask how to switch safely. Liquids may absorb more reliably but can contain sugar alcohols that raise output.

draft.verdict: The bits in your bag could mean the tablet didn't dissolve all the way, or they could just be an empty shell. Either way, please don't stop it or switch to immediate-release on your own. Bring the bits to your pharmacist and ask your prescriber about changing.

why.claim: A tablet or shell seen in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left after the drug was released. It is worth showing the pharmacist, but it does not prove either one.
You are not alone. In one small study, 11 of 50 people with an ostomy had seen undissolved medicine in their pouch.
Your product is an extended-release tablet.
Slow-release tablets can release part of their dose in the colon. Your colon isn't connected, so the tablet has less time and gut surface to release the drug.
Time-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel. If things move through fast, part of the dose may leave before it is released.
How well medicines are absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. You have over 200 cm, which matters too.
The label says these tablets must be swallowed whole and never crushed or chewed.
Immediate-release and liquid forms of carbamazepine are also sold. Choosing one, and how to switch, is a decision for your prescriber, not something to do on your own.
Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can raise output.

swapToAskAbout.text: Guidelines say an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often worth asking the pharmacist about. Only your care team can decide if, how, and when to switch. Please don't switch on your own.

draft.verdict: A shell in your bag could mean the tablet did not fully release its medicine, or it could just be the empty coating, so it isn't proof either way: please don't stop or switch on your own, and call your pharmacist or doctor soon to show them what you found.

why.claim: The label lists this medicine as a film-coated, extended-release tablet.
It has an enteric coating that soaks up water and dissolves as the pH in the gut rises. After that, it releases the drug slowly.

When things move through the gut fast, an enteric coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets pass through whole. So a tablet in your bag is a real reason to check, but it doesn't show for sure how much medicine you absorbed.
In a shorter bowel, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
After a large small-bowel resection, guidelines say extended-release and enteric-coated medicines are generally avoided.
If a medicine doesn't seem to be working the way it should, poor absorption should be suspected and raised with your prescriber or pharmacist.
Guidelines say to talk to a pharmacist before changing the form of a medicine, and that includes switching products.
Absorption changes differ from drug to drug, so each medicine should be looked at on its own with your prescriber or pharmacist.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole and not to chew, divide or crush them.

draft.verdict: Ver la pastilla en la bolsa es una señal importante, pero no le puedo decir si dejarla o cambiarla; esa decisión es de su médico o farmacéutico, así que lleve lo que vio y pregúnteles pronto.

why.claim: Una tableta o cáscara entera en la bolsa puede significar que el medicamento no se disolvió, o puede ser solo la cáscara vacía que queda después de soltar el medicamento. Vale la pena mostrársela al farmacéutico; no prueba ni una cosa ni la otra.
Su pastilla es una tableta de liberación prolongada.
La etiqueta dice que debe tragarse entera, sin masticar, triturar ni partir.
En personas con ostomía, las tabletas de liberación prolongada están en el grupo de mayor riesgo de no disolverse bien.
Con un intestino corto o un tránsito rápido, parte de la dosis puede salir del cuerpo antes de soltarse.
Sin colon, estas tabletas tienen menos tiempo y menos superficie para soltar el medicamento.

Las guías dicen que, tras perder mucho intestino, a menudo vale la pena preguntarle al farmacéutico por una versión de liberación inmediata o líquida del mismo medicamento. Es una pregunta para ellos, no un cambio para hacer por su cuenta.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you to stop it or switch it, but finding the Claritin-D 12 Hour tablet in your bag again is a good reason to show your pharmacist soon, because this slow-release type is generally avoided after a large small-bowel surgery.

why.claim: A whole tablet or shell in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left behind after the medicine came out. Either way it is worth showing the pharmacist, but it doesn't prove which one happened.
This product is an extended-release (slow-release) tablet.
The label says not to divide, crush, chew or dissolve the tablet.
After a large small-bowel surgery, slow-release medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to let the medicine out.
With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave your body before it gets out of the tablet.
Slow-release products may let out part of their dose in the colon. Your colon is not connected, so the tablet has less time and less gut lining to work with.
One source puts extended-release products in its highest-risk group for not dissolving in people with an ostomy. Solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets are in its lowest-risk group.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can increase your output. So a liquid version should be checked too.

why.claim: This product is a liquid (a solution), not a tablet.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome.
Liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol. These pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.

The label text I had lists benzoic acid, hydrochloric acid and potassium bicarbonate, but the list is cut off and the separate inactive-ingredient section was missing. So I can't confirm there are no sugar alcohols.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so plain medicines can often still be absorbed if that part remains.
A review found absorption dropped for 29 of 37 drugs after bowel surgery. It differs by drug, so it can't be predicted for you alone.
When absorption is hard to predict, clinicians may watch the drug's effect closely. For metformin, that could mean checking your blood sugar results.
Guidelines recommend a pharmacist check every medicine's form and inactive ingredients after major bowel surgery. That is the real next step here.
The label says taking it with a meal raised absorption somewhat compared with an empty stomach. Ask your pharmacist how this applies to you.

draft.verdict: I can't act as your doctor or tell you what to do with your Pristiq, and please don't stop or change it on your own. What I can tell you is that it's an extended-release tablet, and without a colon, part of the dose may pass out before it is released.

why.claim: Pristiq is an extended-release tablet.
The label says the tablets must be swallowed whole with fluid, and not divided, crushed, chewed, or dissolved.
Time-release tablets need enough time moving through the bowel to release the drug. If things move fast, part of the dose may leave the body first.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the large intestine. Your colon is not connected, so the tablet has less time and less surface to release the drug.
One ostomy study puts extended-release products in the 'critical' group for dissolving poorly.
How well medicines are absorbed depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma. Having over 200 cm may help you, but it doesn't rule out a problem.
In that same study, over 60% of ostomy patients said no one had told them how an ostomy can affect their medicines. So asking is a normal and useful step.
The label says about 80% of the drug reaches the blood when taken by mouth.

천천히 녹는 약은 장을 지나는 시간이 충분해야 약이 다 나옵니다. 내용물이 빨리 지나가면 약 일부가 녹기 전에 몸 밖으로 나갈 수 있습니다.

장루가 있는 사람에게 서방형 약은 '녹는 데 문제가 생기기 쉬운' 종류로, 바로 녹는 일반 정제는 문제가 덜한 종류로 분류됩니다. 다만 바꿀지는 처방한 분이 정할 일입니다.
남은 소장이 길수록 흡수가 더 잘 되는 편입니다. 그래서 내 몸에서 실제로 어떤지는 의료진이 함께 봐야 합니다.

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

G:pg139#time-release.text: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.

G:remane-2025#formulation-classes.text: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

G:remane-2025#patient-education.text: In the pilot study, 11 of 50 interviewed ostomy patients had seen undissolved medicine, and over 60% said they had not been told how an ostomy can affect their medicines.

G:remane-2025#tablet-in-pouch.text: An intact tablet or shell seen in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve, or it can be an empty shell left after the drug was released. It is worth showing the pharmacist; it is not proof either way.

G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release.text: The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

draft.ask: ASK: I have an ileostomy. Can you show me exactly how to take my nystatin suspension, and check whether it has sugar or sugar alcohols that could raise my output?
sourcesChecked: Guidelines: sugar alcohols in liquid medicines, liquid forms, simple sugars
draft.verdict: I can't act as your pharmacist or tell you how to take your nystatin, even just hypothetically, because that has to come from your own prescriber and pharmacist. What I can tell you is that the label says very little of it reaches your blood, and I still can't tell whether this liquid has sugar or sugar alcohols in it.

why.claim: The label says nystatin is absorbed very sparingly when swallowed, with no detectable blood levels at recommended doses. So it is not a medicine that depends on your gut to absorb it into the blood.
This product is a suspension (a liquid).

The label's description lists only artificial (wild) cherry flavor as an inactive ingredient. The full inactive-ingredient section was missing, so I can't confirm whether it has sugar or sugar alcohols.
Liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can raise stoma output.
Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols draw water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
Concentrated simple sugars such as syrups also draw water into the bowel, and are usually limited with short bowel syndrome.

draft.ask: ASK: I have a colostomy with over 200 cm of small bowel. Can you walk me through how and when to take my Carafate tablets, and what to watch for in my pouch?
sourcesChecked: FDA label: dosage_and_administration, how_supplied, description, pharmacokinetics, information_for_patients (absent or not returned)
Guidelines: Sood 2013, Remane 2025, AGA SBS update, Parrish & DiBaise 2017
draft.verdict: I can't act as your pharmacist or give you step-by-step dosing, and the Carafate label I have doesn't include its directions section, so the exact "how to take it" steps need to come from your prescription label and your pharmacist.

why.claim: The label I can see lists Carafate only as a tablet. It names no extended-release or enteric coating.
The listed ingredients are sucralfate, magnesium stearate and microcrystalline cellulose. I saw no sorbitol or other sugar alcohol in that list.
Plain fast-dissolving tablets are grouped as lower risk for not dissolving in people with an ostomy. Extended-release and enteric-coated products are the higher-risk group.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, so medicines are often absorbed normally. Your stoma type alone doesn't guarantee that.
Something you can do yourself: watch your pouch for whole tablets. In one study, 11 of 50 people with an ostomy had seen undissolved medicine. If you see one, take it to your pharmacist to look at.
Over 60% of people in that study said nobody had told them how an ostomy can affect their medicines. So it's worth asking your pharmacist to go through the steps with you at the counter.

swapToAskAbout.text: ఒక మందు సరిగా శోషించబడదేమో అనిపిస్తే, అదే మందును వేరే రూపంలో వాడే విషయాన్ని కేర్ టీమ్ ఆలోచించవచ్చు. ఉదాహరణకు ద్రవం, నోట్లో కరిగేది, చర్మం మీద రాసేది, లేదా నోటి ద్వారా కాని రూపం. sorbitol లేని రూపం ఏదైనా ఉందా అని ఫార్మసిస్ట్‌ను అడగండి.

draft.verdict: నేను మీ ఫార్మసిస్ట్ లేదా డాక్టర్‌లా నటించి, ఈ క్యాప్సూల్‌తో మీరు సరిగ్గా ఏం చేయాలో చెప్పలేను. అది మీ కేర్ టీమ్ మాత్రమే నిర్ణయించాలి. పైగా ఈసారి "Dimetane" పేరుతో ఒక లేబుల్ దొరికింది, కానీ అది brompheniramine కాకుండా diphenhydramine రికార్డుకు లింక్ అయి ఉంది. కాబట్టి ఇది మీ దగ్గర ఉన్న మందేనా అని నేను ఖచ్చితంగా చెప్పలేను. డబ్బా మీద ఉన్న మందు పేరును సరైన స్పెల్లింగ్‌తో పంపండి, లేదా లేబుల్ స్పష్టంగా కనిపించే ఫోటో పంపండి.

why.claim: దొరికిన లేబుల్ ప్రకారం ఇది ద్రవం నింపిన క్యాప్సూల్ (liquid filled capsule).
ఆ లేబుల్‌లో ఉన్న ఇతర పదార్థాల్లో sorbitol ఉంది. కానీ ఈ లేబుల్ మీ మందుదేనా అని ఇంకా ఖచ్చితంగా తెలియదు.
Sorbitol లాంటి sugar alcohols శరీరంలో సరిగా శోషించబడవు. అవి ప్రేగులోకి నీటిని లాగుతాయి. దాంతో స్టోమా నుంచి వచ్చే అవుట్‌పుట్ పెరగవచ్చు.
చాలా నోటి మందులు చిన్న ప్రేగు మొదటి భాగంలో శోషించబడతాయి. ఆ భాగం మిగిలి ఉంటే, వెంటనే విడుదలయ్యే మామూలు మందులు చాలావరకు ఇంకా శోషించబడవచ్చు.
మందు ఎంత బాగా శోషించబడుతుందనేది స్టోమా రకం కంటే, మిగిలిన చిన్న ప్రేగు పొడవు, దాని ఆరోగ్యం మీద ఎక్కువ ఆధారపడుతుంది.

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

G:aga-sbs#medications-alternatives.text: When a medicine may be poorly absorbed after resection, the care team may consider liquid, dissolvable, topical, or non-oral forms of the same drug instead.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:pg139#sugar-alcohols.text: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

L:inactive_ingredient.text: purified water, sorbitol sorbitan solution … Inactive Ingredients 25mg:- Gelatin, glycerin, polyethylene glycol 400

evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-simple-sugars: Concentrated simple sugars (sweets, syrups, sweetened drinks) draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic: Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-alternatives: When a medicine may be poorly absorbed after resection, the care team may consider liquid, dissolvable, topical, or non-oral forms of the same drug instead.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:pg139#extended-release-avoid: Extended-release products are generally avoided after extensive resection; an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often a question worth asking the pharmacist about.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

draft.ask: ASK: Is it OK for me to take benazepril with my potassium pills, and should my potassium blood level be checked?
sourcesChecked: Guidelines: potassium supplements and ileostomy medicines
draft.verdict: I can't give you a yes. Whether benazepril is OK to take with potassium pills is a drug-combination question, which I can't check, and the label's warnings section was missing, so please ask your pharmacist before you take them together.

why.claim: I can only check whether benazepril itself can be absorbed with your ileostomy. The label calls it a tablet, not slow-release or delayed-release, so that part looked fine.
Plain fast-dissolving tablets are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving problems in people with an ostomy.
The guidelines advise a pharmacist review of every medicine after major bowel surgery. That review is the right place to check benazepril and your potassium pills together.
People with an ileostomy are more likely to get dehydrated and low on salt, and some medicines can add to that risk. This is another reason to have a pharmacist look at your full medicine list.

draft.verdict: I can't approve medicines, and that stays your doctor's call, but for plain furosemide tablets with your anatomy I found nothing in the sources I checked that says to avoid them.

why.claim: This label is for a plain, immediate-release tablet. It is not a timed-release or coated design.
Timed-release and coated pills are the ones guidelines usually say to avoid after bowel surgery, because they need a long gut to release the drug. That concern doesn't fit a plain tablet.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many plain tablets can still be absorbed when that part is still there.
How well a pill is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. Your length isn't known, so how much you absorb is uncertain.
Even in people with a normal gut, the label says only about 64% of a furosemide tablet is absorbed compared with an injection.
No sorbitol or other sugar alcohols are listed. The label does list lactose, and most people with short bowel don't need to avoid lactose.
If the medicine doesn't seem to do what it should, poor absorption may be the reason. Tell your prescriber or pharmacist.
Watch for signs of dehydration and raise them with your team quickly: thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, or more output than usual.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic: Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

evidence.G:pd-2017#salt: Salting food and choosing salty snacks is commonly encouraged in short bowel syndrome with high output, within the care team's advice for the person's heart and kidney health.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.

swapToAskAbout.text: Gabapentin also comes as a liquid. Liquids may be absorbed more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome. But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols, which can increase stoma output. Ask whether the liquid would suit you better.

draft.verdict: Gabapentin is a plain immediate-release tablet, which is the kind of tablet that tends to work best with your anatomy, but with under 100 cm of small bowel it may not all be absorbed, so check with your pharmacist.

why.claim: This product is a plain tablet. It is listed as immediate-release, not timed-release or coated.

The listed ingredients are gabapentin, corn starch and copovidone. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohol is listed. (The separate inactive-ingredient section was missing from the label, so this list may not be complete.)
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain immediate-release tablets can often still be absorbed when that part remains.
Plain fast-dissolving tablets are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving properly in people with an ostomy.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left. You have under 100 cm.
Even in a full-length gut, the body takes up only part of each gabapentin dose. The label says that share gets smaller as the daily amount goes up.
In studies, most drugs were absorbed less after part of the bowel was removed. A few stopped working well. This varies by drug, so no one can say ahead of time how much it will affect you.

final.ask: ASK: I have an end-jejunostomy with under 100 cm of small bowel. Will I absorb enough gabapentin from this tablet, or would a liquid form suit me better, given that liquids can contain sugar alcohols?

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:hong-2021#absorption-findings.text: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.

G:pg139#liquid-forms.text: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

G:remane-2025#formulation-classes.text: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

L:pharmacokinetics.text: Bioavailability of gabapentin is approximately 60%, 47%, 34%, 33%, and 27% following 900, 1200, 2400, 3600, and 4800 mg/day given in 3 divided doses, respectively.

why.claim: This product is listed as a tablet.

The listed ingredients are gabapentin, corn starch and copovidone. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohol is listed. (The separate inactive-ingredient section was missing from the label, so this list may not be complete.)
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain immediate-release tablets can often still be absorbed when that part remains.
Plain fast-dissolving tablets are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving properly in people with an ostomy.
How well a medicine is absorbed tracks how much healthy small bowel is left more than the type of stoma. You have under 100 cm.
The label says the body takes up only part of each gabapentin dose, and that share gets smaller as the daily amount goes up.
In studies, most drugs were absorbed less after part of the bowel was removed. A few stopped working well. This varies by drug, so no one can say ahead of time how much it will affect you.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.
evidence.L:pharmacokinetics: Bioavailability of gabapentin is approximately 60%, 47%, 34%, 33%, and 27% following 900, 1200, 2400, 3600, and 4800 mg/day given in 3 divided doses, respectively.
